#8425. How to Sharpen a Knife: The Ultimate Step-By-Step Guide to a Sharp Blade

Published Oct 27, 2026 11:09 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A knife is perhaps the most useful tool for anyone who loves the outdoors, and learning how to sharpen a knife is an important skill that will take time to perfect. But with some practice and concentration, anyone can learn to keep their knives sharp and ready for the next cutting task. Through years of experience in my knife sharpening business, I’ve developed a system for quickly getting a sharp edge that I’ll share with you in this article. I’m going to give you a step-by-step guide for two methods of knife sharpening: First, with a traditional sharpening stone. Second, with sandpaper and a mousepad. Yes, you read that correctly, a mouse pad sharpener.

There are many great knife sharpeners on the market that are easy to use and effective. But, learning how to sharpen a knife with a stone is a skill everyone should know. Now, there are many options out there for stones which range from cheap synthetic stones that wear out with one or two uses, all the way to high-end Japanese water stones that cost hundreds for each grit. For this knife sharpening tutorial, I’ll be using an inexpensive, but effective, medium natural Arkansas stone that I’ve had for years.

I like to use water on my stones, so I begin by submerging my stone in a Tupperware container filled with water while I prepare everything else. It’s not a good idea to use a stone dry because the metal shavings will “clog up” the stone and make it ineffective. During the sharpening process you may rinse the stone and soak it again. Too much water being drizzled on the stone during the process won’t be a problem, but too little can be. Make sure your stone has plenty of water on it during the entire process.

Take your marker and color the sharpening bevel. This will allow you to see where the stone is contacting the edge so that you don’t go too shallow or too deep. When the marker is gone, you’ll know that you’ve gotten to the apex of the edge.

Hold your knife close to the blade and lay it on the stone with the edge facing you. Place the fingers of your free hand on the spine (back/non-sharpened) of the knife and let the tips hang over and rest on the stone. Keeping your fingers on the same spot and letting them barely drag across the stone will help you keep a consistent angle until you really get the feel for it.

Hold the knife’s spine off the stone at about a 20-degree angle. Only the edge should touch as you make a light pass starting from the knife’s tip then moving across and away on the stone until the heel touches the stone.

Then check where the marker is worn off. If only a narrow line is worn off right at the very edge, your angle was too steep, and you need to lay the blade slightly lower to the stone. If the marker is only worn on the other side of the bevel, you were too shallow, and you need to bring the blade a little higher off the stone. Make a few passes until you find the sweet spot where the entire edge is contacting the stone, then go to Step 4.

Tip: Finding and maintaining a consistent angle is the most difficult part of sharpening with a stone. An angle guide is a handy accessory to buy with your sharpening stone. The guide will keep your angle consistent and act as training wheels as you get used to freehand sharpening.

Now that you have your angle, make passes on the stone until you feel a burr on the edge. Carefully (and lightly) “wipe” your thumb or finger across the edge. Make sure the motion is perpendicular to the edge, not parallel to it. One will allow you to feel the burr, and one will likely slice you.

It should feel “rough” going from one direction and smoother from the opposite direction. Sometimes you can see the burr. It may just look like a micro-bevel that will catch the light, but it’s a tiny “flap” of metal that has been folded over the edge.

When the whole edge has a burr, you can go back to Step 3, and do the same thing on the other side. (When you raise the burr on the other side, the burr may begin to come off and look like a super fine piece of wire as it detaches from the edge.) For most people, the hardest thing about this process is switching hands with the knife. Training your non-dominant hand may take some time. If you can’t get the hang of switching hands, you can flip the knife over so that the edge is facing away from you, and keep it in the same hand. But this will require that you learn the motion backwards. Either way works fine as long as you keep the angle consistent.

After you raise a burr on each side of the bevel, you will want to refine the edge. Make alternating passes on the stone, always with the blade’s edge trailing the spine. I usually do ten passes on the left, then ten on the right, then five, three, two, and one pass on each side. After that, I’ll check the sharpness by slicing a piece of paper. If it goes through it cleanly, then you’re all done. If there are some hang-ups or it won’t slice well, it may need some more refining, or you may not have raised the burr correctly.

Sharpening with a stone will definitely take some practice, and you will mess up more than once. But this is a great skill to develop that will absolutely be worth the time it takes to learn. One last note on using stones: Some people will progress through several stones to go finer and finer. If you do that, just raise a burr on both sides on each stone until your final stone. When the final grit is reached, you can raise your burrs, then refine the edge. Don’t bother refining on any stones other than your final grit.

Sharpening a knife with this sandpaper method will give you a convex edge on your knife. The good news is learning how to sharpen a knife will be easier since you don’t have to keep the angle perfect the entire time. As for the Sandpaper, I recommend the automotive wet/dry type. You can buy them in variety packs with a range of grits that will suit sharpening quite well.

Cut your scrap of wood to 3- to 4-inches wide, and as long as your mousepad. Cut the mousepad to fit the width of the wood and glue the fabric side (the surface the mouse moves on) to the wood. You can do this to both sides of the wood so it won’t slide around on your table. Having the rubber side out helps hold the sandpaper in place. I have used a general spray adhesive and had good results.

Just as with the sharpening stone method, I recommend using a permanent marker to mark the edge bevel on your knife. Color the whole edge bevel so that you can easily see where the paper is removing material. This will help you determine the correct angle in the next step.

The angle is slightly less important with a convex edge because the edge has a curve to it due to the flex in the mousepad base. Even if you are off by a couple of degrees, the pad’s give will cover your mistakes. Lay a piece of 600-grit paper on the block, and hold it in place with your fingertips at the bottom. Hold the knife with the edge facing you and at a 15- to 20-degree angle off the paper. Starting with the tip at the bottom corner, push the knife away from you while sweeping towards the opposite upper corner of the block. Now look at your marker to see where you’re removing material. The same adjustments apply here that I described in the sharpening stone method.

Just as with the stone method, once you find your angle, you will make passes on one side until you raise a burr, then switch sides and raise a burr again. Don’t start with any grit lower than 320 unless you have deep chips or rolls in the blade. The lower grits will remove material quite fast, and you can mess up your blade if you aren’t careful. Also, you don’t need a lot of pressure for this method. Too much will cause a lot of deformation to the pad, and make your convex edge too steep. A lighter touch works best. Remember to be careful with your fingers that hold the paper.

Once you have raised a burr on both sides, you can change the grit and begin to refine your edge. Take the next grit and do ten passes per side (or until you have removed the scratches from the previous grit), then move up and do the same until you’ve reached your final grit, then do ten strokes on each side, and reduce the number as described in the stone method. If you go up to 2000 grit, you will start to get a mirror-polished finish on your blade. If you are diligent about maintaining your angle and hitting the apex, you will have a very sharp knife by the time you reach 2000+ grit. You can get grits of 6000 and above, which will really polish and refine your edge and I can easily get an edge that will whittle hair with this method.

Remember that using this method always requires the edge to be trailing the spine. You can’t make passes where the edge is going into the paper. That can work on a stone, but not here. Also, the paper can be taped to the edges of the wood so that you don’t have to hold it with your off-hand. I generally just hold the paper myself, but you just have to stay aware of where the blade and your fingers are. Although this method is more forgiving than a stone, a consistent angle will yield the best results.

This method should really be called “How to maintain and touch up a knife with a honing rod,” because a honing rod is best for, well, honing an edge. Whether the honing rod is metal (think butcher shop) or ceramic, it’s designed for keeping an edge sharp. They are best when used frequently, between uses of the knife. There are better options for sharpening a dull knife with a damaged edge.

Honing rods can be handheld, or mounted in a tabletop holder. If you’re new to sharpening, or not very confident with holding the knife and hone at the same time, it’s best to go with a tabletop version.

As you make a pass on the hone, you will start off very shallow and gradually increase the angle until you feel the edge just begin to “bite.” This means you have reached the apex, and you will actually be refining the edge, not the material behind it. Repeat this for the other side of the knife, and take note. Keeping the angle consistent is very important.

Once you have found the correct angle, make alternating strokes on either side of the blade. Be sure that as you make your stroke, you are beginning at the heel of the blade, and finishing at the tip. For a handheld hone, your stroke will begin at the far end of the hone, with the heel of the edge, and as you move toward the handle of the hone, you will be pulling the blade back to get to the tip. The motion will be down and outward. Then bring your blade back up, cant it the opposite way, and make a stroke the same way for the other side. Take your time and move slowly. With experience will come speed. For a horizontal table mounted hone, the motion will be very similar. Away from you and outward, heel to tip, then flip the knife so the edge is pointing toward you, and make a stroke toward you from heel to tip.

If you are finding that your blade has lost some sharpness, you may have gone too steep with your angle, or you may be “rolling” your wrist during the motion, which changes the angle. If you have gone too shallow with your angle, there will be no change to the sharpness, because you weren’t reaching the apex of the edge. If you aren’t getting the results you want, try making small changes to the angle you’re using. If you aren’t sure which way to go with the angle, color the edge with a marker, and make a few strokes. You will see where the marker is worn off, and that will let you know how to change the angle. If you have chips or damage to the edge, you may need to use a stone or other method before honing.

Work Sharp makes a wide variety of sharpeners, but this will cover how to sharpen with one of their belt style sharpeners. Using the Work Sharp will give you a convex edge. This is a great way to go as long as you get your technique down. When done properly, it’s not hard to get a near mirror finish on your edge with one of these versatile tools.

Depending on the model you have, you will be able to select from a few different preset guides that will determine the angle of your edge. For thinner knives, like kitchen or fillet knives, choose a lower angle in the 15- to 18-degree range. For pocket knives and general use blades, 20 degrees is my favorite. If you plan on using a bigger blade for heavy chopping or just want a really strong edge, 22- to 25-degrees will work well. Select the guide that will suit you best and clip it on, or rotate it into place, depending on the model.

Is your blade still pretty sharp, but just needs a touch up? A fine grit belt should be your choice. Do you have some small nicks in the edge? Maybe a slightly blunted tip? Start with a medium belt. Does the edge look like you chop rocks for fun? Start with the coarse belt to get those repairs done more quickly. Wherever you start, you will progress through the belts getting finer and finer until you finish.

Turn your Work Sharp on, and if there are different speeds available, select the lowest speed while you are learning. Going too fast, especially with a coarse belt, can remove a lot of material in a hurry, and end up making a mess of your knife. Choose a side of the belt, set your blade against the angle guide, and lower the knife until it contacts the belt. Starting at the heel, pull the knife back toward you, and as you get toward the tip, raise the back of the knife up to keep the belly of the blade parallel to the ground. Be careful though—raising the back too high can result in rounding the tip of the knife. Avoid putting more pressure near the tip than you do at the heel. Go lightly, and let the belt do the work.

It may take a few passes on the same side before you raise a burr. You will be able to feel it with a fingernail, and usually see it on the edge. Once the whole edge has a burr, you’re ready to raise one on the other side of the edge. Repeat Step 3 on the other side of the edge until you have raised a burr.

Once you have raised a burr on both sides of the edge, you can change the belt to the next grit higher (finer). Begin alternating strokes, one per side. Make several passes on each side until you begin to see the scratch pattern from the previous grit disappear. When all you see are the finer scratches, move to the next belt, and repeat. By the time you are done making these alternating passes, and you have worked through the grits, you should have one very sharp knife, with a durable convex edge.

Stropping a knife is the final step in really getting your blade super sharp, and it’s also a great way to maintain your edge between sharpenings. Most strops are made of leather, but there are some cotton and even paper strops available, too. Since a wood block mounted leather is the most common, and, in my opinion, the most effective strop, here’s how to use one to get the most out of your edge.

There are many different compounds available for strops. Like sandpaper, they are rated by their grit. When you buy a leather strop, it’s usually bare, and has no polishing compound in it. You will need to “load” the strop before you use it. There are tons of choices ranging from paste, to bars of compound, to diamond emulsion sprays to load your strop. I generally use the bars, and rub each strop with a different compound from coarsest to finest. You don’t need multiple strops, but most have two sides for a coarse and fine compound. Load your strop with some compound by rubbing it in, or spraying it on, then grab your knife and get ready.

While it’s fine to use a sharpening stone with the edge “biting” into it, strops can only be used with the edge trailing in your stroke. Otherwise, you end up with a sliced up piece of leather and a duller knife. Start with the edge facing you and the heel of the blade fully on the strop. Push the knife away from you and move it outward so that you finish your pass with just the last inch or so of the knife on the strop. Be careful not to roll your wrist as you do this because it will increase the angle and dull the end of the blade. Keep the angle the same as how you sharpened it. After your first pass, lay the blade flat on the strop, roll it over the spine of the blade so that the other side of the edge is now on the strop. Then make a pass with the knife moving toward you, with the edge trailing behind. Be sure to move from heel to tip as you make the pass. This will keep the tip from biting into the strop and damaging it.

When you figure out the motion of stropping, and you see how it takes your edge to the next level, you may get addicted to it. I like to listen to podcasts while stropping my knives. Take your time, and make alternating passes, back and forth and back and forth. You will begin to see that edge really shine, and you can get a near perfect mirror polish on there with good compound, and a little elbow grease. Don’t use too much pressure, maybe slightly more than you do when you’re writing. Let the compound do the work, and enjoy the results. Remember that stropping is also a great way to keep your blades sharp. After each use, hit the strops for a minute or two, and you can go a long, long time between actually having to sharpen the blade, provided you don’t damage the edge too badly while cutting. A few minutes on a good strop can usually straighten out minor edge rolls and get your blade back in shape so you don’t have to remove material by sharpening.

Now that you know the basics of how to sharpen a knife, here are some tips that will help you master the skill.

Letting your knife get to the point where it will hardly cut will make a lot more work for you. If you take a minute every week (or every day, depending on use) to make a few passes and keep your knife honed, you will rarely have to sharpen it. I use a leather strop once or twice a week to keep my knives in shape, and they rarely need a full sharpening like I have described here. Use a strop just like you would the sandpaper method.

A few companies have small angle guides that come with their stones that look like little wedges. These wedges are meant to help you get a feel for the angle. Most come in 17, 20, or 25 degrees. For a beginner, these can really speed up the learning process. Once you get a feel for it, you most likely won’t keep using them, but they are great aids in learning.

It can be difficult to get a consistent angle on the belly (curved portion near the tip). I overcome this by always keeping the edge parallel with the bottom of the stone. At the beginning of the pass, the knife handle will be pointing away from you so that the tip is parallel to the bottom (side of the stone closest to you). As your pass progresses, the handle will end up parallel to the bottom of the stone as you reach the straight part of the edge.

Don’t sit down and try to learn this if you have a lot of other stuff to do. Set aside some time to practice this skill so you can slowly work through it and absorb what you’re doing. Trying to rush through this will frustrate you, and likely yield poor results, or injury.

Everyone has one of those gas station knives kicking around, and they are perfect to practice on. Most come with a terrible edge anyway. If you slip and scratch the surface, you won’t be heartbroken, and if you foul up the edge, you won’t lose sleep. Once you’ve got some confidence, move up to the stuff that matters.

One of the most common mistakes I see is people rolling the knife at the end of a pass on the stone or paper. This will change the angle and prevent you from getting a good edge. At the end of the pass, keep the knife at the same angle and lift straight up to come back for another pass. Your wrist shouldn’t look like you’re twisting a throttle on a motorcycle at the end of the pass. Keep your wrist still. Lift your arm at the end, don’t twist or roll the knife.

Although the examples used here were Arkansas Stones and sandpaper, the same basic steps and principles can be applied to most sharpening techniques, whether they be sharpening a knife with a guided system, like a Work Sharp Knife and Tool Sharpener or a ceramic rod. You still have to establish an angle, raise a burr, and refine the edge. Learning how to sharpen a pocket knife or kitchen knife shouldn’t feel like a mystery, even if there is some art to it. Remember that perfect practice makes perfect, so take your time and focus on getting angle and technique correct, and you’ll be enjoying a sharp edge before you know it.

#8423. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

#8421. Gossamer Gear The Free Tent Review: A Freestanding Double-Wall Tent Under 2 Pounds?

The Gossamer Gear The Free is a one-person, double-wall, freestanding ultralight backpacking tent. Unlike the brand’s traditional trekking-pole shelters, The Free uses a DAC aluminum hub-and-pole system to create a freestanding structure that can be easily repositioned at camp.

Constructed with Gossamer Gear’s exceptionally tear-resistant, PFAS-free nylon fabric, The Free aims to deliver durability and weather protection without unnecessary weight. At just 29.8 ounces, this tent joins the Durston X-Dome 1 and the Nemo Hornet Osmo 1 as one of the lightest freestanding, double-wall tents in the world — and it’s the most affordable of the three, to boot.

But does its minimalist design strike the right balance between weight savings, comfort, and practicality on the trail?

After taking The Free on a section hike of the Continental Divide Trail in northern New Mexico, I came away impressed by its weather-resistant construction and sturdy design. However, its narrow dimensions and some setup quirks left me wishing Gossamer Gear had not sacrificed quite so much interior space in the pursuit of ultralight performance.

I tested The Free during a section hike of the Continental Divide Trail in northern New Mexico, during which the weather was frequently miserable and wet. The conditions gave me an excellent opportunity to evaluate the tent’s weather protection, condensation management, and overall durability.

One of the most noticeable differences between The Free and my previous shelters was its double-wall design. I appreciated being able to avoid the persistent dampness that comes from brushing against a single-wall tent’s interior in wet conditions. In addition, a few nights were particularly windy, and I was impressed by how solidly The Free held up.

However, my overall experience was mixed. I felt that The Free lacked the interior roominess I’ve grown accustomed to in The One. Despite being a relatively small user, I often felt cramped and occasionally claustrophobic.

The Free’s DAC aluminum hub-and-pole system distinguishes it from Gossamer Gear’s traditional trekking-pole shelters. The tent can stand without stakes when pitched with its inner mesh body, making it possible to move the shelter to a different spot before securing it.

Like most freestanding tents, the fly requires staking out the vestible for proper tension, and additional stakes for guylines in less-than-ideal conditions. While the freestanding design sounds wonderfully convenient, I found the initial setup more complicated than expected.

Gossamer Gear developed a custom ultralight shelter fabric called ClearSkies. It combines 15D recycled Robic fabric with a 20D dope-dyed ripstop silicone/polyurethane coating. The company designed this material to improve strength and waterproofing while avoiding PFAS.

The fabric has a reported hydrostatic head rating of 4,923 mm — waterproof enough to withstand heavy downpours and wind-driven rain. The seams are factory-taped.

The fabric is manufactured using a dope-dye process, which incorporates color into the polymer before the fibers are formed. This can improve colorfastness compared with conventional surface dyeing and reduce water and energy consumption during manufacturing.

In the field, the fabric felt reassuringly robust for such a lightweight shelter. During wet and windy conditions, I appreciated the protection it provided without the bulk or weight of a heavier tent.

Although the double-wall construction kept me from directly touching the wet fly, moisture accumulated on its underside, particularly when I kept the vestibule closed to retain warmth overnight. By morning, the fly could be soaked and noticeably heavier.

The fly also sits close to the inner mesh body, helping maximize the available interior space. Unfortunately, that limited separation meant that contact between the inner tent and the wet fly could transfer moisture inside. The Free offers the advantages of a double-wall shelter, but its compact geometry makes condensation management especially important.

The Free’s inner mesh body must be pitched first. Two aluminum poles connect through a central pivoting hub that attaches to the inner tent’s ceiling, creating the tent’s basic structure.

This inner-first setup became a drawback in rainy weather. While I worked to get the fly in place, the mesh interior was exposed to the elements. Since the fly was often still damp from the previous night, assembling the shelter without adding more moisture wasn’t always easy.

The color-coded poles and corresponding corner attachments help guide assembly, but I struggled to keep everything in place while inserting the poles into their designated corners (often with comical results). In breezy conditions, the lightweight tent threatened to slither away before I could finish setting it up. I initially tried holding the corners down with my feet, but eventually resorted to staking them down. That rather defeated the convenience I had expected from a freestanding tent.

The Free is reasonably straightforward once you become familiar with its pole arrangement, but I wouldn’t describe the setup as effortless, especially when the weather is uncooperative.

As I mentioned above, The Free felt more cramped to me than Gossamer Gear’s The One, which I have used extensively. Although the two tents have similar floor dimensions (The Free is even a few inches longer and wider), The Free has a significantly lower peak height and the angle of the side walls feels more restrictive.

The Free has a tapered floor measuring 34 inches wide at the head and 21.5 inches at the foot. At 86 inches long, it’s long enough for most solo backpackers, but the narrowing floor is a significant consideration when choosing a sleeping pad.

My pad fit comfortably, with a little room to spare. However, anyone using a wide sleeping pad should check the dimensions carefully. Per Gossamer Gear’s website, “while The Free’s floor dimensions don’t technically support a traditional 25″ wide pad, it does fit — it’ll just push the side walls a bit. For the best fit, we recommend going with a wide tapered pad instead.”

At 5 foot 7, I could sit upright and even stretch my legs inside. Still, I frequently brushed against the sides or top of the tent. When the fly was wet, those accidental touches could bring moisture into the living space. The compact dimensions are understandable in a shelter designed for minimal weight, but the trade-off was more noticeable than I expected. I often felt confined, particularly when spending extended periods inside during bad weather.

Gossamer Gear lists a maximum user height of 6 feet 2 inches, but height alone doesn’t tell the whole story. Sleeping-pad width, sleeping position, and how much room you want to sit up or move around all influence how comfortable this tent will feel.

The D-shaped doors open into a modest vestibule with enough room for my backpack and a few smaller items. This was useful for keeping gear protected from the weather without cluttering the sleeping area.

My main complaint was the vestibule door’s toggle system. When rolled back and secured, the door tended to hang into the tent rather than staying neatly out of the way. One morning, I cinched it closed with the toggle, only to have accumulated ice fall directly onto my sleeping bag. Magnets or a more effective door-retention system would have made this detail less frustrating.

The Free includes two interior pockets: one near the ceiling and another beside the door. While I appreciated having somewhere to stash small essentials, I found the pockets less useful than expected. Items tended to slide out, making it difficult to keep things securely organized. For an ultralight tent, the storage options are welcome, but I would have preferred pockets that hold their contents more reliably.

The Free impressed me with its sturdy pole structure and durable-feeling fabric. It handled windy conditions well, and the double-wall design provided a welcome barrier between me and the wet fly.

However, the fly’s tendency to collect condensation and its close proximity to the inner mesh deserve consideration. Proper ventilation and careful pitching are important, especially in cold, damp conditions.

This was the tent’s biggest weakness for me. Although I could sit up and move around to a limited extent, the tapered floor and close-fitting walls made the interior feel cramped. Taller users and anyone carrying a wide sleeping pad should pay particular attention to the dimensions.

The color-coded pole system makes the design reasonably intuitive, but pitching the inner tent first can be inconvenient in rain or wind. I also found myself staking the corners during setup to keep the lightweight body under control.

The freestanding structure is useful, but it doesn’t eliminate every need for stakes or make the pitching process as simple as I had hoped.

At 29.8 ounces, The Free is impressively light for a double-wall, freestanding shelter. Its compact packed dimensions make it an appealing option for backpackers who want to keep their pack weight down without switching to a trekking-pole shelter.

The ClearSkies fabric feels like a thoughtful balance between low weight and ruggedness. Despite its delicate-sounding 15-denier thickness, the material is designed for improved tear resistance, and I was impressed by the tent’s overall robustness during my hike.

The use of recycled Robic fabric and PFAS-free materials is a welcome feature. The dope-dyed fabric construction is also designed to improve colorfastness. These choices make The Free appealing to backpackers who want a lightweight shelter without overlooking material considerations.

The Free comes with six aluminum stakes, four guylines, a pole-repair section, a stuff sack, and a pole bag.

The Gossamer Gear The Free makes a compelling case for an ultralight, freestanding backpacking tent. And while it isn’t the featherweight champion when compared to minimalist trekking pole shelters, The Free is still one of the lightest tents in the freestanding double-wall category. At $400, it wins heavily on its value-to-weight ratio. However, its impressive weight savings come with noticeable compromises in livability and convenience.

If minimizing pack weight is your top priority, it deserves a look. If comfort and easy setup matter just as much, I would consider a roomier alternative.

The Gossamer Gear The Free was donated for purpose of review.

#8419. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8417. Best Lever Action Rifles of 2026

Published Oct 27, 2026 12:56 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

When I was a kid, there were three reasons I wanted a lever action rifle. First, they were cool. Second, because I grew up just outside New Haven, Conn., the historic home to Marlin and Winchester, they were my hometown guns. Third, they were cheap.

Only one of these things is still true. Lever guns always have been and always will be cool, though they will never again be cheap, nor—barring divine intervention—will they ever again be produced in Gun Valley.

Writing about the top lever action rifles is a bit tricky. Do you focus on the best of all time, which is great for us nostalgic sorts, or do you talk about great lever action rifles that you can buy new?

I tilted this list of the best lever action rifles in favor of those you can order new. Though if you have a hankering for one of the old-time classics, there are plenty to be had on the used market. Just don’t expect to find any bargains. Nearly all quality lever actions command a premium.

This list is divided into those guns that are being currently produced (or soon-to-be) in significant numbers and those that are either specialty orders or that must be sought out on the used gun market.

With the exception of the rifles that have just been announced, Senior Staff Writer Tyler Freel and I have shot, handled, and/or owned all the models listed. Beyond our hands-on experience with the rifles over the years, however, many of them are no-brainers based on their well-documented history and legacy.

The good — actually, great — news here is that we’re seeing more lever actions made with each passing year. About 15 years ago, Remington screwed the pooch with Marlin and those were some dark days indeed. In those years it seemed only Henry was making quality lever guns in meaningful numbers, but things have taken a turn for the better.

Under Ruger’s ownership, Marlin seems poised to flourish. Henry is still innovating hard and trotting out new models in new cartridges, like the 360 Buckhammer. And we have a couple interesting and innovative newcomers in the mix.

When Ruger resurrected Marlin, the first model they brought back was the 1895 SBL. This was a smart move because the SBL, with its gray laminate furniture, stainless steel metal, threaded barrel, oversized lever loop, and picatinny rail was one of the sexiest and most sought-after iterations of this classic lever action.

I had good things to say about the Marlin 1895 SBL when it was reintroduced in late 2021, and that opinion hasn’t shifted. It is the best lever action rifle produced under the Marlin brand—at least in the modern era. Packing 6+1 rounds of .45/70 Gov’t in its magazine, it brings a formidable level of firepower to the party which is why it has garnered a lot of interest from hunters in bear country, as well as with everyday sportsmen in more sedate parts of the U.S.

Marlin has also introduced two new versions of the 1895 worth considering, a Model 1895 Trapper and a Model 1895 Guide Gun. The Trapper comes with a Skinner peep sight, no picatinny rail, and is a bit more compact (34 ¼ in. vs. 37 ¼ in.) than the SBL. It, too, is chambered in .45/70 and has a 5+1 magazine capacity. The Guide Gun (model GBL) is slightly less expensive than the SBL ($1,239 vs. $1,479), has traditional semi-buckhorn sights, blued steel, is chambered in .45/70, and a 6+1 capacity.

In 2024, Smith & Wesson made a big splash in the lever-gun world with their model 1854. It was first introduced in .44 Magnum, and .45/70 models followed suit in 2025, along with options in the venerable .30/30 Winchester and .45 Colt.

We were immediately impressed by the first Model 1854 rifles we got our hands on. These lever guns, which are relatively complex pieces of machinery, were superbly executed — with excellent fit and finish and smooth operation. They feature both side-gate and magazine tube loading, and are available in blued/wood and stainless/synthetic trims. Both are generally classic-looking styles, but the synthetic version offers modern perks like a picatinny rail, M-Lok slots on the fore-end, and a threaded muzzle. Since introduction, Smith & Wesson have also introduced a Stealth Hunter model with black-on-black finish, a longer optic rail, tactical-style handguard with multiple M-Lok slots, and threaded muzzle — specifically for optics, lights, and a suppressor.

We’ve tested several of the Model 1854 rifles as they’ve rolled out and have been consistently impressed with the quality of build, smoothness of operation, and reliability of these guns. We rank them among the finest factory lever guns made today.

One of the slickest, funnest lever guns we’ve ever run is the Lever Action Supreme from Henry. This rifle combines the nostalgia and classic good looks of a lever gun with some features that a lot of modern shooters will find appealing. It’s offered in both 5.56/.223 and .300 Blackout, and its most notable characteristic is that it feeds from standard AR-15 magazines. Since it’s introduction, it’s also been updated to include the popular .450 Bushmaster. This isn’t simply a design that Henry adapted to work with these mags and cartridges. They started from scratch.

The Lever Action Supreme cycles very smoothly and uses an AR-style rotating bolt head and the bolt body does not protrude from the rear of the receiver as with many other lever guns when cycled. It also sports a floated barrel that provides good accuracy and while it has a classic look when bare, it’s equipped to accommodate modern accessories like suppressors, scopes, and red dot optics. You can read Snow’s full review of the Lever Action Supreme for a more detailed look.

It didn’t seem that long ago that Henry Repeating Arms was only making Golden Boys chambered in pistol cartridges and .22s. But these guys have been busy, and as the company embarks on its second quarter century, they have added an impressive number of products to the lineup.

One of the flagship hunting rifles is the All-Weather Picatinny Rail .45/70 Side Gate, which is Henry’s version of a do-everything guide gun. As the name implies, it is built for the elements. The metal has a hard-chrome satin finish. The stock is a stained hardwood.

It has an aperture peep sight mounted at the rear of the substantial Picatinny rail. Henry outfitted it with an oversized lever loop. With the 18.43-inch barrel, the overall length is 37.5 inches and it has a 4+1 capacity. The rifle can be loaded either through the side gate on the receiver or by dropping rounds into the tubular magazine.

This is a versatile and capable thumper that is equally at home in bear country or in a deer stand overlooking a food plot.

The Winchester Model 1873 might have been The Gun that Won the West—a great bit of marketing by Winchester executives—but the Model 94 is undeniably the rifle that won the hearts and minds of generations of deer hunters. If you polled long-time hunters regarding their choice as the top lever action rifle, there’s little doubt the Winchester 94 would win the vote.

This was the most prolific of Winchester’s lever actions, being the first sporting rifle in the U.S. to sell a million units. Prior to the end of its domestic production in 2006, more than seven million Model 94s were produced.

Model 94s are still being made for Browning/Winchester by Miroku Corp. in Japan and are available in several different grades. These run from the basic Carbine (1,309)withitsplainwalnutstockandbrushedpolishedbluedmetal,totheDeluxeSporting(2,230), which has case color hardened metalwork, upgraded wood, nicely executed checkering, and a half-round, half-octagonal deeply blued barrel.

Currently, the 94 is being offered in .30/30 Win., .38/55 and .450 Marlin.

The Browning BLR is one of the most versatile lever actions on the market. It is available in both short- and long-action lengths and because it feeds from a detachable box magazine it is able to run pointy spitzer-style bullets in cartridges usually associated with bolt guns.

The Lightweight ’81 Stainless Takedown is the most utilitarian BLR of them all, making it the best lever action rifle in the BLR family. It breaks down into two pieces for easy transport and is built on a lightweight aluminum receiver and sports a stainless steel barrel for excellent weather resistance. At about 7.25 pounds (depending on the specific chambering) it has a very nice balance and feel. Combined with its smooth lever system, which uses a clever gear and pinion design, the BLR embodies the lithe, fast-handling characteristics that lever action fans admire. (I’d be remiss if I didn’t give a nod to the legendary Winchester Model 88, which was a game-changing lever action from which the BLR drew lots of inspiration.)

The Lightweight ’81 Takedown is currently chambered in .243 Win., 6.5 Creedmoor, 7mm-08 Rem., .308 Win., .300 WSM, .30/06, and .300 Win. Mag. Several other cartridges are available in other BLR models as well.

It’s difficult for me to express how happy I am to include the Marlin 336 among the top lever action rifles currently made. I know I’m not alone in this. I cut my teeth hunting deer with a Marlin 336 in .35 Remington so, as with countless other hunters, the 336 was my first love.

We’ve handled and put a few rounds through one of the new 336’s, which will initially be chambered in .30/30 Win., and its quality was spot-on. As with the 1895s, the 336s have excellent fit and finish, run smoothly, and are aesthetically pleasing.

As you history buffs probably know, the original Henry lever action was the first commercially successful lever action rifle. Originally chambered in .44 Rimfire, it was one of the most advanced firearms to see action during the Civil War and was fielded in limited numbers by Union Troops.

Confederate Colonel John Mosby is credited with cursing it as “that damned Yankee rifle that can be loaded on Sunday and fired all week,” after fighting against troops wielding it in battle. That unintentional endorsement stuck and helped propel the Henry to everlasting fame.

Henry makes a “New Original Henry” chambered in either .44-40 WCF or .45 Colt, though the most popular (and affordable) homage is the Henry Golden Boy rimfire, which can be had in .22 S/L/LR, .22 Mag., or .17 HMR.

In .22 LR, the most popular configuration, the rifle holds 16 rounds, the same as the original. It has a 20-inch octagonal barrel that is nicely blued and contrasts sharply with the bright “Brasslite” finished receiver and brass buttpad and barrel band.

The receiver comes drilled and tapped for a scope, but before you mount an optic on yours spend some time running it with semi-buckhorn sights, as the Creator intended.

These Golden Boys run like a scalded squirrel and can digest ammo by the brick over the course of an afternoon.

As a first gun for a youngster, it has no real equal. But its appeal is so strong that no one will fault you for buying one for your grownup self first.

In 2024, Savage introduced the Revel, a rimfire lever-action chambered in .22 LR, .22 WMR, and .17 HMR. Considering their modest price, these are great little lever actions. They come in three trims: Classic, DLX, and Tactical.

I’ve had one of the classic Revels for a couple years and it’s a wonderful balance of traditional looks, performance, and modern features. It’s got handsome walnut furniture with a couple of modern lines and nice ergonomics. The steel has a matte blued finish, and the aluminum receiver is coated in black as well. The DLX has wood furniture with some modern M-Lok slots and the gun has a threaded muzzle. The Tactical version has black synthetic furniture.

The classic version I’ve been shooting has traditional dovetailed sights and the slightly heavy weight of the barrel, in conjunction with the buttstock design, makes the rifle quick to the shoulder and steady pointing. The receiver is unique in that it features two push pins that can be used to take the rifle down in seconds for stowage or cleaning. A lot of our .22 LR ammo is excessively waxy, and that can gum up lever guns pretty easily so easy takedown is helpful.

The Tactical Revel comes with a Picatinny rail for mounting an optic, but the other models are drilled and tapped to accommodate a scope. These are some of the nicer rimfire lever guns you’ll find for the money today.

The Marlin 1894 was hot stuff when it was introduced back in the day. It was the first lever gun with a flat top, side-eject design that anticipated the eventual wide-spread adoption of telescopic sights on rifles. This innovation gave it a leg up (on paper anyway) compared to the Winchester 1894 which debuted at the same time, though the fact that the Winchester came in the potent .30/30 versus the less powerful offerings in the Marlin gave Winchester’s 1894 a decisive advantage.

The Marlin 1894 has been chambered in a variety of mostly pistol-caliber cartridges over the decades, the most common of which (in the modern era) included the .44 Spl./.44 Magnum. .38 Spl./.357 Magnum and .45 Colt. I have a North Haven, Conn., built 1894 in .44 Magnum and it is one of my favorite carbines. (Though if I could snap my fingers and conjure any 1894 it would be one chambered in the quaint and now obsolete .218 Bee.)

Ruger announced the return of the Marlin 1894 this spring, so we will hopefully have hands-on range time with one soon for a full review. Expect to see the first offerings in the cartridges mentioned above, but as details become available we’ll update this information. (Note: the rifle pictured above is one of the older Marlin 1894s).

Rossi has recently, with the R95, become a true contender in the .45/70 lever gun space. Their stainless-steel R95 Laminate .45/70 is a high-quality gun that incorporates some modernized features and is better quality than even some of the previous Marlin models. This model has a polished stainless receiver — that is honestly a bit over-polished — and laminated wood furniture. They seem durable and weather-resistant in our testing, but we’d prefer the fit of the fore end to be a bit better. The sides of it aren’t fully against the magazine tube and can flex and potentially crack.

This new .45/70 lever gun features a modernized M16-style extractor and a threaded muzzle for accepting a suppressor. Staff writer Tyler Freel put a lot of ammo through his sample and it ran beautifully. You can read his full review here. Priced below some of the top-shelf lever guns like the new Marlin, Henry, and Smith & Wesson rifles, it’s affordable but still very good quality.

Another great Rossi lever gun is the Rio Bravo .22 LR. This is available in a number of configurations, but we really like the wood/gold variant. This is a lever gun with good looks that isn’t priced to be a safe queen. Staff Writer Tyler Freel put one of these to the test with his son and you can read his full review here.

The Rio Bravo has an aluminum receiver with a top cover that’s held in place with four Phillips-head screws. It’s easily removed for cleaning and maintenance — something that’s important to keep rimfire lever guns working correctly. It’s an accurate rifle that works well with a variety of ammunition and holds 14 rounds in its tubular magazine. If you want to mount an optic, you can use the narrow dovetail atop the receiver with tip-off rings, but this gun is most fun with iron sights.

This list could have been much longer, but in the interest of brevity I’ve only highlighted a few notable classic lever guns. Before getting to those, however, I do want to highlight a couple important honorable mentions.

The Spencer repeating rifle is one. It was the first military repeating rifle that used self-contained metallic cartridges and is the forefather of all lever actions. Though the Spencer was produced for only a short time (1860 to 1869) and in relatively limited numbers, it was the steppingstone upon which the lever action rifle, specifically Winchesters, was built.

The Winchester 1895, which gained prominence as Teddy Roosevelt’s “Big Medicine” in .405 Winchester is an iconic lever action whose fame outstrips its actual benefits. From a technical standpoint, its most distinguishing element is that it was the first Winchester lever action fed from an internal box magazine.

This was the first big-boy lever action in history. The Winchester 1886 changed the game because its strong locking-block action was able to handle proper rifle cartridges, rather than the pistol rounds that previous lever action designs were limited to.

It was originally chambered in .45/70 and .45/90, two rounds you can still get it in. Over the years it was loaded for other hard-hitting rounds like the .50/110 Winchester and .33 WCF.

Those rounds, combined with its excellent handling characteristics, made the Model 1886 the first true big-game capable lever action. Today, you can order it in a Saddle Ring Carbine configuration (1,630)witha22-inchbarrel,in“ShortRifle”trim(1,450) with a 24-inch round barrel, or go all out with the fancy Deluxe Case Hardened model ($1,930) with a 24-inch octagonal barrel, upgraded walnut and color case hardened receiver.

Arguably the finest lever action ever (and if there’s one thing lever gun fans like to do its argue about which is best), the Savage Model 99 was a revolutionary addition to the American sporting scene when it was trotted out in 1899.

It had an elegant, hammerless design, used an innovative rotary magazine that allowed the rifle to safely chamber cartridges with spitzer-style pointed bullets, and a stock silhouette that oozed sexiness and speed decades before such aesthetics became the hallmark of art deco industrial design.

First called the Model 1899, it officially changed to the Model 99 in 1921 when the .300 Savage was introduced. Initially, the 1899 was chambered in .303 Savage and .30/30 Win. Soon, Savage added other cartridges to the lineup—the most iconic of which was Charles Newton’s speedster, the .250-3000 Savage, in 1915. Later in life, the Model 99 added the .243 Win., .308 Win., 7mm-08 Rem., .375 Win. and others to the mix.

My Model 99 is a particularly lovely rifle. It was given to me by my father-in-law before he passed away and is a takedown model chambered in .300 Savage that includes a .410 bore barrel that it shoots single-shot.

The rifle was sold by Abercrombie and Fitch to legendary car maker Carroll Shelby, who eventually gave it to my father-in-law as a gift. It’s still in its original case of leather and wood lined with purple velvet. I rarely shoot it—but admire it frequently.

Though it never gained the following of the Savage 99, the Winchester Model 88 is similar to the Savage in that it incorporated a lot of technical innovation in its design and caused hunters and shooters to reassess the lever action platform.

Winchester unveiled it in 1955. It had a short lever throw and used a rotating three-lug bolt that smoothly stripped rounds from the detachable box magazine. The Model 88 was chambered in a handful of cartridges that were new at the time, specifically the .308 Win., .243 Win., .284 Win. and the .358 Win., which was a particularly terrific brush round that is sadly all but forgotten these days.

The Model 88 has a hammerless design and side eject, which allows for easy mounting of an optic on the receiver. One particularly clever feature is how the trigger moves with the lever loop, eliminating the possibility of a pinched finger or snagged glove when working the action.

I don’t think there’s a rimfire lever action as beloved as the Marlin 39A. It tops many shooters’ lists as the best .22 LR ever produced. The legacy of the 39A is fascinating. It started as the Model 1891 and was the first .22 LR lever action produced. Its legendary accuracy was demonstrated by Annie Oakley who used one in her shooting exhibitions. The Model 39A held the distinction of being the longest continually produced shoulder-fired firearm in history. That streak was broken when the dimwits who purchased Marlin and placed it under the Remington umbrella decided to move Marlin’s production facilities from North Haven, Conn., to Ilion, New York—at which point the production of all Marlins ground to a (predictable) halt.

My sincere hope is that we’ll soon—as in the next couple years—be able to reclassify the 39A under the “Best Lever Action Rifles Being Currently Made” category since it seems Ruger is doing such a fabulous job reviving Marlin since they purchased it.

When you think “cowboys” and the “Old West” the first rifle that comes to mind is this beauty. The Winchester 73 really was the right gun for the right time—being the first rifle chambered for the .44-40, which is said to be the first centerfire cartridge developed. Whether it deserved to be called “The Gun that Won the West” as Winchester touted, there’s no denying that the Model 73 was used to send a whole bunch of men—both good and bad—to their maker, and accounted for innumerable deer and other game to boot.

The Model 1873 was produced until 1923 but has enjoyed a revival since the sport of cowboy action shooting sprang up. Uberti makes replicas chambered in .357 Mag. and .45 Colt, while Winchester, which worked with their Japanese partner Miroku, has been importing ’73s since 2013. Those are available in .357 Mag., .45 Colt, and .44-40 WCF.

Since the barrel of a lever action is longer than that of a handgun, cartridges like the .357 Mag. and .44 Mag. get a significant performance boost in terms of velocity that makes them more capable on animals like deer and hogs.In addition, a lever-action chambered in .357 can run .38 Spl. rounds, which are economical and have little recoil making it a great option for plinking and practice.

Yes. They are fast-handling, quick-shooting, easy to wield and carry, hold good quantities of ammo, are available in a wide range of cartridges for different applications, and are legal in most all jurisdictions. Whether you’re on horseback with one in a scabbard or have a take-down model in a bug-out bag, lever-actions are an excellent choice.

Are lever-actions effective on dinosaurs?

Absolutely. The Marlin 1895 SBL carried by Chris Pratt’s character—dinosaur whisperer Owen Grady—in Jurassic World, would be a top choice as a dino stopper, provided it was loaded with heavy, hard-hitting ammo like Buffalo Bore’s 380-grain mono-metal WFN dangerous-game load.

Certainly. A carbine-length lever action chambered in a pistol cartridge like .357 Mag. or .44 Mag. would be a highly effective option for home protection. Even a rifle chambered in .22 Win. Mag. can be a formidable home-defense gun when loaded with ammo like Federal Punch.

Usually when one compiles a “best of” list—whether talking deer rifles, elk cartridges, or sniper rifles—there is significant push-back with the selections. Everyone has deeply-held convictions on such matters.

With lever action rifles, it is a bit different. There are many rifles that are universally agreed upon. No one in their right mind is going to say that a Savage 99 isn’t one of the best lever action rifles of all time. The same goes for the Model 94, Marlin 336 and others.

I think we rally around lever actions because they are the quintessential American rifle. Yes, we make the best bolt-actions in the world, and the same can be argued with other firearms platforms—but the lever action is distinctly ours. Though some are made abroad and imported, the lever action is, and always will be, America’s rifle.

John B. Snow is Shooting Editor of Outdoor Life, where he oversees the publication’s firearms and shooting coverage. This includes gear reviews, features on technical innovations, stories on shooting techniques and general hunting coverage with the occasional fishing story thrown into the mix.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8414. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8411. An Old-School Perspective on Finding Better Duck Hunting: Get Creative and Target the Hardest Places

Published Oct 27, 2026 3:00 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The way some hunters talk, you’d think good waterfowl hunting was a thing of the past. Sure, it was great 25 years ago. You could pick almost any field or pothole and shoot a limit of ducks. But millions of ducks and geese still sweep the flyways each fall, and a determined hunter can find good shooting. It’s just that you have to hunt the hard places.

That’s my name for spots that teem with ducks and geese but rarely see a hunter. Sometimes these areas demand too much effort, but more often hard places are open expanses that offer a hunter no place to hide. Pastures, the favorite haunts of Canada geese, are one example. How can you blind on a pasture as flat as a billiard table? A flooded field also is a problem. Hunters line the dikes of flooded stubblefields like fence posts, but few of them head for the middle because there’s no place to hide. The potential for open-water hunting on lakes, reservoirs, and bays, where waterfowl raft by the thousands, has hardly been touched. The windswept expanses of open ice where geese frequently rest has great possibilities too. In some parts of the United States a person has little choice about where to hunt. But in many regions, particularly in the prairie and Western states, hard places with excellent hunting abound.

Most hunters credit ducks and geese with too much intelligence. Some waterfowlers would have you believe that the Canada goose, for example, is second cousin to Einstein. That image of brilliance is ridiculous. Geese and other birds are smart just as dogs are smart. To teach a dog to sit, you push his rear down and say, “Sit!” After a few lessons he’ll sit when you give the command. Waterfowl learn similarly. On heavily hunted lands waterfowl avoid cover because they’ve learned that’s where the shots come from.

In much open country they’ve had no such conditioning. No one has shot at them, so ducks fall over themselves to land in decoys placed far from cover. In the hard places, waterfowl aren’t conditioned to be cautious. That is the basis for good bird hunting. It also accounts for the fact that you don’t need much of a blind in the open. Hunting hard places is more a matter of philosophy than of technique. Once you’ve decided to hunt a hard place you’ve cleared a major hurdle. Then you just get out there and start hunting. To show how simple it is, I’ll tell you about some ways my friends and I have hunted the hard places.

I usually don’t use a blind. In my part of Oregon, Canada geese spend a lot of time feeding and resting on pastures, and most ranchers don’t want their sod dug up for blinds. A blind above ground also is about as conspicuous as a high-rise apartment building. The only option is no blind. So you just lie on the ground.

Any hunter knows movement really spooks waterfowl, so being able to disguise yourself as a frozen clump of mud is the big step in making this work. I usually clump a few goose decoys around my body and put one in front of my face. The oversize shell decoys made today are especially good for this kind of hunting. A friend of mine has made silhouette decoys that are so large he can curl up behind one. In late season, when swans are present, I’ve used large swan silhouettes among my duck and goose decoys. This technique has worked especially well on ice, when I’ve worn a white suit and lain behind a swan silhouette.

Put your decoys as far from ditches and weed patches as you can. Set up where birds don’t expect danger. Look for small depressions, places where the grass is lumpy, or pressure ridges on the ice so you can hide. Even a slight variation will make you less obvious. And wear clothing that looks like the ground. The obvious choice after a snowfall would be to wear a white suit or to cover yourself over with a sheet. When the cover is green, pull a square of green camouflage cloth over yourself. Some of the pastures I’ve hunted in are muddy. My hunting coat is so impregnated with dirt it looks like part of the ground, so I often don’t cover myself with anything. An occasional roll in the mud keeps the blind fresh.

On windy days this simple approach is almost foolproof. The birds fly low and come directly in from the downwind side. Obviously you want to lie on the upwind side of a decoy. On calm days when waterfowl fly higher and sometimes circle, it’s not as easy, especially if you gawk at them.

In my region farmers flood their grainfields after harvest. Flooded fields draw ducks the way a candy store draws kids. For years I pondered the featureless expanses of water and mud, trying to figure out how I’d get out there without sinking out of sight forever. Then it struck me—an air mattress. Along with a huge bag of floating decoys, I dragged a well-inflated canvas air mattress into a partly flooded field. With the decoys downwind, I flopped the mattress on a clump of mud and lay on it, face up, and pulled a piece of camouflage cloth over me. Ducks and geese nearly landed on me. An air mattress will do the trick in any soggy spot where you can anchor it to some ground. But don’t try it in deep water.

A rubber raft is best for deep water. I use a two-man, rubberized, olive drab canvas raft. You can find these at big sports stores or surplus stores.

The raft can be dragged or carried to any location, and it often serves where a rigid, heavy duckboat won’t. I’ve used it in the same fields I used to hunt with an air mattress. It also works well in marshes where only a few inches of grass show above the surface of the water. I got this idea from watching a hunter one day in a flooded stubblefield. He had a low-profile boat, which he covered with chicken wire. He tied stubble all over the wire, then crawled under it into the boat. His simple blind looked like a mat of straw lying on the water. Ducks swarmed into his decoys as if he weren’t there.

From that example I made a chicken-wire cover for my raft, with a flap cut out of the middle so I could sit up and have an area to shoot through. I tied short pieces of decoy line on the chicken wire and used these to tie grass, stubble, lily pads, and other appropriate plants to the wire. In addition, I cut a floor for the raft made of 3/8-inch plywood. With some spar varnish for weatherproofing and a strip of outdoor carpet stapled around the floor’s edge to keep it from chafing the raft, I had a rigid bottom that made the raft stable. I can sit, kneel, or stand in it without much wobbling.

Another item that could be used in the same way as the rubber raft is a float tube, or belly boat. While these are made for fishing small waters, they’re well suited to hunting. I recently got one with a camouflage cover, and it looks like part of the marsh. With a chicken-wire cone covered with tules, it would look just like a muskrat house.

If the water is too shallow to use a float tube in the conventional manner—with your legs dangling in the water—you can use it as a shooting platform. One friend, Dave Hummel, did something similar with a tire inner tube. Dave saw lots of pintails on big marsh ponds. Those educated birds weren’t about to land within shooting range of the tule fringes, where a hunter could hide. They stuck to the middle of the huge ponds, where the only cover was a few patches of lily pads that stuck up a few inches above the water. There was no way to blind a boat out there, and a person couldn’t lie down in the foot-deep water. So Dave wired a round piece of plywood to the top of an inner tube. To hunt those smart pintails he threw his decoys onto the open water and put his inner tube table in the lily pads. He laid his gun and shells on the platform and camouflaged it with lily pads. Dressed in chest waders he was able to kneel behind it. To hide from circling ducks, he put his face down on the platform. When ducks were within range, he rose on his knees to shoot. Tough shooting? Yes. But it was the only way to get within range of those ducks, and Dave got his share of them.

I recently fished with a fellow who had a “boat” called a Bass Tracker Bantam. It’s a flat plastic hull about five feet long made for poking around backwaters for bass. It’s very stable and rises no more than six inches from the water. It looks to me like an ideal piece of equipment for hard-place hunting.

Another friend hunted from shallow water by using a piece of heavy brown plastic. The water, matted with weeds, was only three or four inches deep. He laid a 12×12-foot square of plastic on the water and jumped into the middle of it. The weeds held up the edges of the plastic to keep water out and he was able to lie down to hide from ducks without getting wet.

Open water may be the extreme example of a hard place to hunt. These days, with many huge reservoirs next to croplands, lots of ducks and geese rest on wide water. A sink box is the answer, but sink boxes are illegal. The next best thing is a low-profile boat. You can’t hide such a boat so you try to make it look like floating debris. My friend David Hagerbaumer hunts extensively on open bays along the Pacific Coast. He uses a Barnegat sneakbox, a flat boat that looks like a miniature hydroplane. Dave has a net for the boat that camouflages it, and he puts seagull decoys on the decks. On open water the boat just looks like a piece of flotsam drifting on the bay. Dave lies on his back in the boat, facing his decoys, which are downwind. This rig works well on diving ducks, and Dave often takes puddle ducks and brant while hunting from it too.

On an incoming tide, puddle ducks often work the shores of estuaries to feed on the flooding beaches and tidal marshlands. That’s when Dave hunts the edges, and he camouflages his boat by tying grass to the net covering, or by shoveling mud clumps onto the decks.

Dave has another rig, called an alligator, that should really do the job for you on mudflats or beaches. These are no longer available commercially, but you could easily make your own. The alligator is a fiberglass coffin, shaped like a mummy with an oblong hole cut out of one side. You drag it out to where you want to hunt, dig a hole, and bury the thing, except for the opening. Then you crawl in, lie on your back, and face up through the hole. It’s no more than a way to stay dry while hiding in a soggy place, but that’s all you need in the hard places.

Hunting hard places can be a little wet and dirty. A rugged, heavy pair of chest waders and a canvas coat that can withstand abuse are necessities. The right gun also is important. Guns get muddy in hard places, and most autoloaders I’ve used turn into single shots under these conditions. A pump gun is OK because you can grind shells through even if the gun does take on a load of grime, but the best choice is a double barrel, which is nearly impervious to dirt. Invariably in hard places you must shoot lying on your back, sitting, or from your knees. Your feet may be stuck in the mud, and you’ll feel like you’re caught in a spiderweb when you start trying to shoot through a chicken-wire cover. Add to that a good stiff breeze, which ducks can use to get quickly out of range, and you have a shooting challenge. A good idea is to practice shooting claybirds from awkward positions, also lie down and practice throwing your gun to your shoulder and swinging it. You may want to learn to shoot both right and left-handed so you can handle ducks coming in from both sides.

Hard places generally call for big decoy spreads. In open expanses, ducks in particular congregate in huge swarms. I can pile about five dozen inflatable ducks on my rubber raft so that’s about my maximum, but more decoys would be even better.

The last day of the season a couple of years ago typifies hard-place hunting. Ducks were streaming into a flooded stubblefield and hunters lined the dikes around the field. I waded out to the middle, found a small patch of mud to lie on, and threw out some decoys. Mallards broke their necks to get into that spread. But the mud was sticky and the wind was howling. By the time I could sit up to shoot, the ducks usually had flared to long range. The one box of shells in my pocket accounted for only four mallards and a honker. But it was an unforgettable afternoon of duck hunting. While hunters pass-shooting from the dikes only took an occasional high bird, I was at the center of a swarming, teeming mass of ducks.

Read Next: Duck Hunting’s New Reality: It Will Keep Getting Tougher for the Workaday Waterfowler

Great hunting still does exist. It demands some ingenuity and hard work. But if you hunt the hard places, you’ll find the birds. And that’s what duck hunting is all about.
