#8409. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8407. SHT Day 12: Castle Danger

Today started out pleasant enough! Who can complain about waking up dry and warm, with a toilet, and even a microwave to warm up one of my butter brioche waffles? These are something new I’m trying on trail and they haven’t disappointed. I even brought along maple syrup. It provides just the sugary kick I need sometimes in the afternoon. Having breakfast washed down with an energy drink, and I’m rearing to go!

The motel owner called me at about 8:40 to see if I was ready, which I was, so we got about a 10 minute head start out of town. She insisted on taking me on a little tour around town first. I wasn’t about to say no after all the kindness she’s shown me, and besides, I’m always willing to see and learn something new. She drove me down to the water’s edge to show off where all the giant cargo ships dock, and around to some of the local businesses, including the brewery. I’ll have to try to fit in a visit to that one at a later date.

She got me back to the trailhead shortly after nine, and I expressed my gratitude to her again. She was incredibly sweet and helpful. The trail started off as a .5 mile road walk on Highway 2 before turning off into the woods along snowmobile track. The first four miles or so were very smooth, at times winding along Silver Creek, where I stopped for an early lunch at its namesake campsite.

The trail follows picturesque Silver Creek

The first four miles were easy. The end of the day was easy and had me winding along the Gooseberry River mostly downhill. The middle portion of the day? Well, that’s a different story. Those miles were easily the most difficult of the trip so far.

This trail register looked brand spanking new

I came across something earlier this morning known in the guidebook as “rock cliff.” I should have taken that as a warning of what was to come later. I was nearing a section of trail known as Castle Danger. The middle 10 miles of trail for my day consisted of very steep ups and downs, at times a legit rock scramble, and hella rocks and roots.

Hard to tell here, but the trail drops off this “rock cliff”. Sign of things to come!

My pace slowed to a crawl. To make matters worse, I shorted myself on water a bit, and it was a hot day. I was getting frustrated and moody, so I had to firmly remind myself to just sit and have a snack. I have a funny mindset on this trail that I want to take breaks only at the official campsites. This mentality sometimes keeps me from doing things that I would otherwise do at any appropriate time that I actually need to do them, i.e., filter water, sit down for a minute, have a snack. This time, I just found the next fallen tree that I could sit on and forced down some food.

This trail marker cracked me up. The arrow is showing that I really do just go “UP”, not straight ahead.

Mood turned! Also, a few miles later I ran into a hiker who shared some water with me and gave me positive news about my next few miles. That was just the motivation I needed.

I ended up hiking 17 miles today despite the late start and tough terrain. I hope I didn’t wear out the ol’ knees and achilles! All told, the Castle Danger section was actually really interesting and would be a really cool day hike. Having a light or no pack would make the scrambles so much fun. I also saw my first significant wildlife today, a beautiful, big-bodied buck, and a cute little snake. As I look back through my pictures, I’m reminded too, that this section afforded me absolutely beautiful views of the landscape and changing colors.

No zoom needed here. I almost stepped on the little fella.

Crossing an unexpected dry river bed in this cool canyon.

Tonight I made camp at Middle Gooseberry Campsite. There are four Gooseberry campsites clustered close together here (west, east, middle, and just Gooseberry). The first one (west) was unappealing and east had a giant group already there. The next one, middle, was small and had two tents and three people staying, but I couldn’t go another step. The next campsite was another mile away and off trail. I was able to find a suitable spot to pitch my tent and make dinner as the sun set on my challenging day.

#8405. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8403. The 9 Ways That Mature Bucks Are Different Than Other Deer

Published Oct 27, 2026 4:29 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Almost every deer on the farm is on its feet. Bucks and does of all ages are hammering food sources. They’re hungry after the rut, but there’s also a snowstorm incoming. Temps are dropping, and there’s a flurry of snowfall — and activity.

Even though the entire herd appears to be on its feet, one buck is still holed up in his fortress. It’s broad daylight, frigid, and snowing. The 5-year-old you want to kill refuses to leave his bedding sanctuary. He’ll move in daylight — all deer must move eventually — but not until it gets closer to dark.

It’s been said many times, but a deer and a mature buck are two different animals.  Older bucks don’t just have more inches of antler on average — they have more wits, senses, and experience. You don’t get to be a five-year-old deer without learning how to survive in the wild, and that’s why these deer not only look different but behave in ways that don’t often align with the does and younger bucks we’re used to seeing. Here’s how.

Hunters can use many physical signs to estimate a buck’s age, but the key I often look for is a buck’s muscle definition. Older whitetails look vastly different than their younger cohorts. Mature bucks have a muscled-up body structure that younger deer just don’t have. As deer progress through each age bracket, they exhibit different body structures.

For example, yearling bucks look like small does with antlers. Two-year-old bucks look like large does with antlers. Three-year-old bucks exhibit a more muscular frame but aren’t filled out just yet. Four-year-old bucks show significant swelling, with heavy shoulders and an enlarged brisket and neck. Five-year-old bucks and older exhibit even more body weight with heavy swelling of the neck, shoulders, and brisket. They might even begin displaying a pot belly and swayed back. Practice judging age in the field, and you’ll be able to better recognize an old buck when he shows up.

Every set of antlers is unique, regardless of the buck’s age. Still, as bucks reach older age classes, they express their genetic code and capabilities. Often, this leads to antler character traits that are usually present in older deer, regardless of the overall score or size of a deer. Examples include kickers, stickers, drop tines, and other unique antler points. It can even lead to greater numbers of points and other interesting non-typical characteristics. Even as they age and their antler size may decrease, older deer still tend to have more mass than younger bucks, particularly around the bases of their antlers.

Deer don’t have personalities in the human sense, but researchers have identified behavioral preferences that we can think of as personalities — particularly when it comes to their movements across the landscape. Some bucks are homebodies or wanderers. (One study found that 33 percent of bucks had a mobile personality.) And as bucks reach older age classes, these personalities can become even more apparent. For example, bucks might be more aggressive or passive. They might be more or less engaged in the rut. Perhaps they even express preferences for specific food sources. If you can start to identify those tendencies and preferences, you have a better shot of patterning your buck.

A common myth suggests that bucks increase their home ranges as they age. For the vast majority of whitetails, this isn’t true. Numerous studies have determined that whitetail buck home ranges and core areas actually decrease in size as they get older. As they become more familiar with their surroundings, they learn the safest areas, best bedding, premier food sources, and more. This leads to a more distinct and deliberate use of the landscape. Hunting older bucks requires finding these smaller areas and home ranges and hunting them accordingly.

As bucks get older, they become more in tune with their environment. They learn where hunters focus their efforts (we humans can become patternable and predictable) and how to avoid us. Older bucks use the landscape to their advantage, especially from a safety perspective.

For instance, bucks use thermal hubs, the low points in the topography where scent collects from the surrounding area. In other words, they don’t necessarily have to walk just downwind of your stand to know there’s a hunter in the area.

Another example includes bucks bedding in ways that give them a security advantage. For instance, mature bucks often bed on leeward ridges, ridge endings, bench edges, and more. Bedding in certain ways allows them to see danger coming from a distance while also smelling any threats upwind that could approach from behind them.

Bucks are also good at finding trails and travel routes that elude stand locations, blinds, and other hunting setups.

Let’s dig even deeper into a buck’s bedding habits, all of which are proven methods that help mature deer detect danger before it detects them. From a scenting perspective, deer find many ways to benefit from prevailing winds and daily thermals.

Using Advantageous Terrain: Bucks tend to bed in areas with advantageous terrain. These locations give them better visibility but also provide winding advantages. As noted above, hilly and mountainous terrain allows deer to use topography to their advantage, but even flatland whitetails find ways to do this. Often, deer that bed in flatter creek or river bottomlands bed close to the water.

For example, deer routinely bed in oxbows. A location with water on three sides helps diminish the odds of a predator approaching from those directions. And if they do, deer can hear them coming through the water. Meanwhile, they can see danger that comes by way of land. If something does approach, deer can bolt out the back door and across the water to safety.

As mentioned above, bucks tend to express a unique personality type. Within those individual preferences comes varied responses to hunting pressure. Human intrusion impacts every deer differently, but most mature bucks don’t tolerate much of it. If they do, they’ve likely been conditioned to certain activities on the property. In other words, some mature bucks may tolerate more pressure than others, but in general, mature bucks won’t tolerate all of it.

Though all bucks are biologically motivated to participate in the rut, some individual bucks can be more active than others. Depending on an individual buck’s tendencies, they might be very active and move a lot during daylight, or they might be reclusive, searching for does at night and bedding back down before daylight.

Read Next: Best Hunting Rifles, Tested and Reviewed

Numerous expert hunters I’ve talked to agree on one particular thing — bucks are hardest to hunt from ages four to six. Often when a buck hits seven, eight, or older, they seem to become more active during the daylight. Perhaps they become overconfident, get delusional and senile, or maybe they just care less. Regardless, they move more and get easier to kill again, almost as a 3-year-old buck would.

Hunting old bucks requires different approaches and tactics than hunting deer in general (does and younger bucks). So, put together a good plan this season, and tag that old buck that’s been haunting your dreams.

#8401. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8399. The Thousand Year Old Trail

“If from today I do not continue walking on your path,.. I have arrived nowhere.” Prayer of La Faba (Pilgrims Prayer)

Europe was in the middle of a record-setting heatwave, and with limited  air conditioning in local lodgings, our room had none. It was a warm, restless night. Knowing we had to climb 2,000 feet in the first 4 miles today, we set off early—though we didn’t quite realize how hard that climb would be.

We started our climb at 7:00 a.m. accompanied by the soothing sound of a bubbling creek about a hundred feet below us.

At first, we walked up a steep, narrow paved road with deep scratches in the asphalt. “Snow chains?” I wondered. I’d soon realize what actually caused those marks.

Before long, the Camino veered off onto a beautiful forested dirt path. Birds sang in the trees, and the creek continued to bubble below. The trail took a steep turn, leveled off briefly, and then pitched sharply upward. This section felt similar to climbs on the Appalachian Trail:, steep, deep woods, dirt, and rock strewn paths.

The key difference from the AT? This path was over a thousand years old.

Massive trees with 15-foot-diameter trunks had guarded the trail’s edge for centuries. The path was worn so deep into the earth that the dirt walls on either side rose up to 20 feet high, fortified in places with ancient rock retaining walls. It was steep, dark, and beautiful.

I stopped to admire one massive old tree that had sheared off about 10 feet above ground. Refusing to give up, a dozen new shoots flared into the air from its stump—some a foot thick on their own. Trees are truly amazing.

Popping out of the forest, we entered the ancient medieval village of La Faba. The village church sat on the hill above—mostly in ruins  except for its standing bell tower.

It was here that we saw the horses that scratched the pavement earlier today. Hikers can schedule horses rides up this steep section of the Camino, something we definitely plan to try if we return. Riding up this ancient road and exiting the forest into a medieval town on horseback must be an extraordinary experience. So this is what caused the scratches on the pavement earlier today

La Faba was built directly into the mountain, featuring thick stone farmhouses with cow barns on the lower level and living quarters above. Potted plants decorated the rock porches of this working farming town.

Leaving town, we recentered the forest on an old cobblestone trail. The path climbed steeply before opening into a broad, rolling mountain meadows. Cowbells rang off in the distance from grazing herds. The views were expansive, revealing valleys and peaks.

Moving on, we stopped in Laguna, a tiny hamlet high up in the hills. We found a small café for caffeine, fresh-squeezed orange juice, and toast.

After our break, we hit a dirt farm path lined with stone walls and soon crossed the boundary into the province of Galicia—our home on the trail for weeks to come.

By 10:00 a.m., framed by a dark spruce forest and a welcome cool breeze, we reached O Cebreiro. A man in a kilt playing bagpipes greeted us as we walked into town.

O Cebreiro features classic Celtic oval structures with thatched roofs (pallozas). Though ancient, the town looks immaculate. Tourists milled about alongside pilgrims—many day-visitors skip the hard climb we had just completed to come straight to this village.

We visited the simple cathedral in town. Something about it made me deeply emotional. It may have been the grueling climb we had just finished, or perhaps it was reading the Prayer of La Faba displayed inside. I’ve seen grand, elaborate cathedrals on this trip, but this humble one touched me the most.

Before leaving, I tried a cortado—Spanish espresso with a splash of milk to lower the acidity—and we stopped to chat with several pilgrims we hadn’t seen in days.

Leaving O Cebreiro, the path meandered through woods with sweeping valley views before following a paved road down to a small crossroads called Linares. We grabbed yogurt and popcorn outside a local store to refuel.

The Camino then diverted back onto a dirt path through the woods, climbing to Alto San Roque. Here stands a 10-foot-tall bronze statue of a pilgrim facing into the wind. He looks as though he had just completed the same grueling walk from Herrerias.

Pilgrims had decorated the statue’s feet with bandages—including heavy tape over his heels to represent blisters.

Moving along the ridge, fields of white daisies swayed in the wind on both sides of us.

We passed through Hospital, another small farming hamlet where locals carried on daily life—driving tractors and hanging laundry—just as villages have done for a thousand years while millions of pilgrims walked past.

The final climb of the day was brutal: just two-tenths of a mile long, but climbing at a slope equivalent to over 1,500 feet per mile. Exhausted, we took tiny baby steps to make it up the incline.

Over the crest, we were delighted to find a small bar waiting right on the trail at Alto de Poio.

We sat down and had our first truly great pilgrim’s meal of the trip:

When we asked for two glasses of red wine, the owner brought us a full bottle! We relaxed and watched other exhausted pilgrims crest the hill, looking just as bewildered as we were by this trail side oasis.They all smiled brightly when I clapped for them as they reached the top.

Feeling rejuvenated, we hiked mostly downhill into Fonfria, a working medieval village where we’d spend the night. We carefully dodged piles of fresh manure on the narrow cobblestone streets.

In Spain, checking into accommodations requires registering your passport and signing paperwork. When we arrived, the internet was down, and the sweet host spoke no English. After some patient gesturing, we got everything sorted and headed to our room to drop our packs.

With little else to do in town, we spent the afternoon hand-washing our clothes and resting in the warming sun.

That evening, our host—who reminded me so much of my Italian grandma—cooked us another incredible meal: steak, fresh salad, fries, Galician cake, and another bottle of wine.

Over dinner, we had a wonderful conversation with Chung Sow, a fellow pilgrim from South Korea, while a herd of cows wandered past us in the street outside.

It was a physically taxing day, but we fell asleep grateful for this little corner of Galicia. We vowed to always seek out cow-poop-covered streets in our future stays!

Although I may have travelled all the roads, crossed mountains and valleys from East to West,  if I have not discovered the freedom to be myself, I have arrived nowhere.

Although I may have shared all of my possessions with people of other languages and cultures; made friends with Pilgrims of a thousand paths, or shared albergue with saints and princes, if I am not capable of forgiving my neighbour tomorrow, I have arrived nowhere.

Although I may have carried my pack from beginning to end and waited for every Pilgrim in need of encouragement,  or given my bed to one who arrived later than I, given my bottle of water in exchange for nothing; if upon returning to my home and work,  I am not able to create brotherhood or to make happiness, peace and unity, I have arrived nowhere.

Although I may have had food and water each day, and enjoyed a roof and shower every night; or may have had my injuries well attended, if I have not discovered in all that the love of God, I have arrived nowhere.

Although I may have seen all the monuments and contemplated the best sunsets; although I may have learned a greeting in every language; or tried the clean water from every fountain; if I have not discovered who is the author of so much free beauty and so much peace, I have arrived nowhere.

If from today I do not continue walking on your path, searching for and living according to what I have learned; if from today I do not see in every person, friend or foe a companion on the Camino; if from today I cannot recognize God, the God of Jesus of Nazareth as the one God of my life, I have arrived nowhere.

#8396. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

#8395. Elk Hunting from ATVs Has Gotten Out of Hand

Published Oct 27, 2026 5:24 PM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I’ve always been a pretty “go with the flow” type of hunter with a general mindset that if it’s legal, there’s nothing wrong with it. But then I went elk hunting on public ground during Colorado’s first rifle season.

I made the 28-hour drive from my home in Pennsylvania to Colorado with my cousins for their first-ever elk hunt. I had warned them of the side-by-side presence I’d experienced on a previous archery hunt in this very unit. It was manageable then. Plus, we’re from PA so we’re used to hunting pressure.

But as our elk hunt progressed, I felt no small amount of anger and sadness as the backcountry we were trying to hunt became a side-by-side racetrack.

We arrived several days before the opener to set up camp, scout the nearby creek drainages and finger ridges, and find the elevation band the elk desired. After a long hike up and into some national forest ground, to my elation, we found a pile of elk. We spotted a few raghorns, a couple smaller satellite bulls, a bugling herd bull, and his harem of cows. They were all using a knob near a meadow for their mid-day bedding area.

We watched them for a bit, then backed out of the area to continue our scouting mission. After zeroing in on the terrain features and elevation a few more times over two days of scouting and finding new elk in each location, we were feeling good about our opening day plan. When the alarm went off in my tent at 3:00 a.m. that morning, we were ready to get started on our 4-mile hike into the target area. As daylight set in, we were already at the bottom of the creek, letting the thermals pull our scent down and away from where we expected the elk to be.

We spent the next three hours meticulously crawling through the creek bottom, checking the north and south facing slopes on each side of us. To our surprise, we never laid eyes on an elk by the time we crested the knob mid-morning. I was a bit confused, until we rounded the corner and a mere 300 yards from where we had seen the large herd was a guide camp with generators, side-by-sides, a large tent with woodsmoke rolling out of the stovepipe, and several easy-ups.

I was frustrated, but I kept my composure and assured my cousin that what those guides were doing was legal and this kind of thing happens. They had accessed the spot via a legal access road that snakes up and around the basin we were hunting. My guess is, they had no idea they had effectively spooked an entire herd of elk by setting up their camp in that location. We hiked away from their camp in search of the elk, but were unable to locate them that day. I counted it as a learning experience for us — if a place is legally accessible by vehicle, we should expect vehicles to be in there.

The next morning, we executed a plan I’d devised lying in my sleeping bag the prior evening. After some obsessive map study, I felt as though I might know where that herd of elk was pushed to. We made our approach and found the herd. Unfortunately, my cousin’s scope had been knocked off zero and he ended up making a non-fatal hit on a nice bull at only 125 yards. His shot resulted in only a few drops of blood and broken spirits. We later found out that his rifle was shooting a foot low.

After re-sighting the gun and mentally recovering, we made our way to a nearby trail to begin our hike to the next pin on my map. The trail had a big sign that read, “Administrative Route — Motorized use allowed only by Forest Service Authorization.” As our trekking poles squelched down into the fresh, muddy UTV tracks, I gave a quizzical look to my cousins. Moments later, a side-by-side came ripping up the trail behind us with two hunters hauling a dead bull. We congratulated them, and they regaled us with their hunt.

“We were just driving around when all of the sudden a whole herd took off in front of us, I threw the gun out the front window and ‘BOOM’, dropped this guy on the run!”

I’m sure my face said a whole lot more than I could muster in that moment, because after that, they quickly said goodbye, good luck, and drove off. Aside from shooting out of a vehicle being illegal in Colorado, it’s just unethical and lacks any respect for wild bull elk, which is a critter that I hold in high regard.

As we continued down the trail shaking our heads in disbelief, three more side-by-sides ripped past us. Our boots became caked in mud as we walked out of the basin, contemplating our next move. That afternoon, we loaded our truck to find a new area. To our dismay, we counted more than 50 side-by-sides either out and about, or parked near tents or campers along the main road through our unit. Every trail was rutted up, and the national forest had seemingly become a UTV mudders’ paradise, except these mudders were pursuing elk.

We also encountered certain trails that were closed only to certain motor vehicles, with a width restriction in place. In essence, any vehicle under 50” was allowed through, and any wider would be stopped by two large metal poles on each side of the path. Unsurprisingly, the poles were bent out to high hell, allowing vehicles much wider than 50” to baja their way through the forest.

By the end of the third day of our hunt, we were disheartened. We had been in elk every day, and able to evade the side-by-side pressure. At times we were even able to use it to our advantage. But we were not enjoying anything representative of a wilderness hunt. The lack of respect for the place and the animals that lived there really started to eat at me.

Read Next: Roadless Areas Provide 10 Times Better Elk Hunting and Support the Best Trout Streams in the West, Study Shows

As someone who grew up in the most hunter-dense state in the United States, I’ve experienced a lot of folks taking shortcuts and not wanting to put in the physical effort to go hunting “the old fashioned way.” However, driving their four-wheelers to their stands on private land is a whole lot different than ripping side-by-sides for miles on supposedly closed national forest roads in pursuit of an elk near the trail.

What draws Eastern hunters like me to the West and to elk hunting is the wilderness. The untouched, unkempt backcountry where humans don’t frequent. Where you can walk up on blue grouse and where the creeks are devoid of cairns and boot prints, where you can witness animals in their natural habitat and their natural state. We dream about silence that almost hurts your ears, the yellow aspen leaves trickling down in a slight breeze, and the snow-capped peaks looming on the horizon. Most of us want our Western hunt to be wild and we want elk hunting to be hard.

Elk deserve to be hunted by woodsmen who read the terrain, watch their wind and thermals, and stalk carefully into range. Elk should not be relegated to some trailside target practice.

I look forward to, train for, and dream about my annual elk hunt for 11 months and 3 weeks every year. Maybe I’ve over-romanticized the beauty and wildness of elk hunting in my mind. But I also know I’m not alone.

There are many of us who welcome the hardships that come with a lack of sleep, long miles, steep climbs, and heavy packs. After all, that’s what makes filling an elk tag so rewarding.

So take the perspective of one Eastern elk hunter for what it’s worth. We should be prioritizing enforcement of off-road rules in our national forests and not letting the off-roaders run amok. We should not be cutting new roads into the little remaining backcountry that we have left, simply because we can. And we need to refocus on what elk hunting, real elk hunting, is supposed to be about.

Derek Horner is the manager of audience development for Outdoor Life where he manages OL’s social accounts and email campaigns, and shares our stories with the world. He was born and raised in central Pennsylvania where his father and grandfather taught him to hunt and fish. He graduated from Pennsylvania State University in 2018 and still lives in central Pennsylvania.

#8394. British Adventurer Karl Bushby Completes 28-Year, 31,000-Mile Hike Around the World

British explorer Karl Bushby has officially crossed the finish line of a 28-year-long hike around the world, returning to his hometown of Hull, England on Monday after walking more than 31,000 miles from the southern tip of South America to the United Kingdom.

The former paratrooper set out on the self-funded trip, which he called the Goliath Expedition, on November 1st, 1998 from Punta Arenas, Chile. He was 29 years old. Bushby had two strict, self-imposed rules: no motorized transport of any kind to advance his path, and no returning home until the entire continuous line was finished.

Now, at 57, Bushby has made it back home.

Originally projected to take roughly 12 years, extreme geographic hazards and geopolitical stalemates pushed the timeline to 28 years, as Bushby crossed four continents and nearly 30 countries. He navigated the infamous Darién Gap between Colombia and Panama, survived an unprecedented 2006 foot crossing of the frozen Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia, spent nearly a decade negotiating Russian visas and Siberian winters, and was jailed twice for illegal crossings.

To maintain the unbroken continuity of his route around conflict zones like Ukraine, Bushby completed a 31-day open-water swim across the Caspian Sea. He then secured clearance from French authorities to swim the English Channel, landing at Shakespeare Beach near Dover in October 2026 before completing his final 250-mile leg north to Hull.

Karl Bushby at his recent homecoming celebration in Hull. Photo: Hullian111, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

While the homecoming was celebrated internationally, Bushby has spoken candidly about the psychological weight of finishing. After spending nearly three decades on this project, adjusting to life back home without the overarching purpose of his trip will be a different kind of challenge.

“My purpose and reason for living is about to end,” he admitted prior to his arrival. “It’s going to be difficult … trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”

A crowd of hundreds gathered outside Hull City Hall and lined local streets to greet Bushby as he pushed his trademark gear cart through town. He completed the final steps of the route at his mother’s home before sharing an emotional reunion with her on the sidewalk after a decade apart.

“They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said to the crowd after finishing. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team: Earth.”

With the trek concluded, Bushby becomes the first person on record to complete an unbroken, continuous foot journey of this scale across the globe. Artifacts, route logs, and gear from the 28-year expedition will go on public display in Hull starting this week.

Featured image: Crowds gathered to welcome Karl Bushby home in Hull, England. Hullian111, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

#8389. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

#8388. The Appalachian Trail: ECT Week 9

The day has finally come to wrap up the International Appalachian Trail. It has definitely been a unique experience though there was a lot more road walking than I would have preferred. For now, as stage one in my grand journey I will appreciate it for what it was. I’m up and out of camp by 5:40am. Though today will be shorter I have made it my goal to get into the town of Millinocket before the post office closes at 4pm to grab a box my parents sent me. All that stands in my way is about 20 miles of hiking and a 40 minute drive into town. I am most worried about that drive into town. The trailhead where I will pop out after my hike is a bit out of the way though any cars that pass by will only have one option to go into town. There just has to be cars that pass by in the first place.

Today begins with a series of exposed rocky sections. At the top of a few it becomes a bit confusing where to continue on as the cairn stones are very tiny, but on one of these sections I am granted my first view of the backside of Katahdin. Mama K. I am getting so close to the Appalachian Trail now. Not much stands in my way. Hopefully in a day’s time I will be standing atop of Katahdin getting ready to begin my journey along one of the oldest hiking footpaths. I cannot overstate how much I have been dreaming and looking forward to finally starting this trail so seeing the mountain on which it begins has me feeling very emotional. Even though I have 1,600 miles under my belt so far on this journey the IAT was just the warm up. The AT is the main event which will have me, Lord willing, standing atop Springer Mountain in Georgia 2,200 miles away as a triple crowner: a backpacker who has hiked the AT, PCT, and CDT. For now, that seems a long ways away so I just focus on getting into Millinocket on time.

I have one river ford to deal with before making my way along a series of long overgrown and neglected old forest service roads. I make good time until I am confronted by a juvenile moose. I try slowly encroaching into his area to get him to push on, and he runs away. I turn the corner to find him looking over his shoulder with what can only be interpreted as a “now what?” face as he hides behind his much larger mother who is fully facing me and staring me down. Alright, you win. Take your time. I’ll just be here taking a video of you. Wait. Come back. If you ever want wildlife to get going just pull out your phone to try and record them. They always seem like they thwart any plans to get a cool video.

Another half hour has me standing at the intersection of three roads where the IAT ends. No cool sign or terminus. Just one last blaze I take a picture next to. Well, that’s over. Add it to the list of trails I have completed. I have had time to digest the trail since finishing, and I have to say it is probably my least favorite trail I have completed. I don’t hate it, and I am happy to have the experience of hiking it. Though, too often, I found myself wondering what I was doing while walking along a thin road shoulder as cars zoomed by. If you are out there to find a true nature experience it will be few and far between on this one. Then when you are on trail for the most part it’s fairly swampy. Except for Quebec. Quebec had the best of everything. Great trail, great huts, great national parks, great food. Anyone looking to get a taste of Canada via the IAT should just do that 400 mile section.

I’m not trying to be too negative. I really enjoyed the people I met along the way. I enjoyed walking into and out of pretty much every town for resupply. In fact, I only ever had to hitchhike to the northern terminus in Newfoundland and into Charlottetown, PEI. I even enjoyed some of those lonely stretches of road which probably hadn’t seen a car come through in quite some time. Frequently, I would get the impression I was discovering some long lost fishing village, or that I was the first person to step foot in a place for quite some time. I like that feeling of being on the outskirts of civilization looking around with fresh eyes. You tend to notice more.

Mostly, I will miss the water. They don’t call some of those provinces the maritimes for nothing. I will miss having the steady presence of the sea. In the beginning in Newfoundland, I looked out at the horizon and wondered how far away Greenland was (turns out about 800 miles as the crow flies). I would see icebergs floating by. The constant presence of fishing boats going about their business, and the gulls that would circle by looking for scraps. Many of the roads I walked along would be littered with lobster traps and other fishing paraphernalia. Oh, and the seafood! One could get spoiled by the amount of seafood I consumed.

But I left all that behind when I turned inland in Quebec. I will have to walk a pretty far ways down into Florida before all that returns. For now, I have the mountains and the green tunnel of forest that surrounds them. I have an odd 14 miles or so of no man’s land between the end of the IAT and the start of the AT. During this section I walk along Katahdin Lake and marvel at the beauty of one of the shelters there. It has canoes at the shelter for people to use during their stay. Another few miles finds me waving in and out of dense overgrown trail following a series of flags and cairns. At this point, I am so used to poorly marked trail I don’t even slow my pace as I weave in and out, up and around as if I know perfectly where I am going. It seems to work as I reach an intersection with a nice, wide, easy two track. You can always tell you are getting close to the parking lot when things become incredibly easy. Also, when you start seeing more trash.

Katahdin Lake in the background. Maine has quite a few lakes to enjoy.

Here, I befriend an older gentleman who is just finishing up some volunteer trail work. We walk together for a bit before I say my goodbyes and try to push onwards to the trailhead parking lot. Well, I should have just hiked with him as he comes wandering out of the trail as I am still trying to hitch and offers me a ride into town. It is 3pm and it takes about 40 minutes to drive to town. The post office closes at 4pm. I swear it is always a race against time with the post office on trail. Luckily, I make it with 15 minutes to spare. He then drops me off at the hostel where I check in.

Thanks to the AT Hostel for all their help. A great place to stay.

I’m staying at the Appalachian Trail Hostel for two nights. I have worked it out so I will get a shuttle back into Baxter State Park in the morning, climb up Katahdin via the backside, traverse the Knife’s Edge, summit Katahdin and start the AT, summit Hamlin Peak (my first AT side quest), then descend down the far side and get picked back up and taken into town. The next day I will get dropped off where I left off. I will then attempt to hitch to the west side of Baxter State Park to climb North Brother mountain and then hitch back again and continue on to the start of the 100 mile wilderness. These two side quests have been stressing me out for a while. A large part of me wants to attempt to do all of this in a day and not go back into Millinocket, but I know that would be a very long day both in miles and especially in elevation. I think I better play it safer in the middle of a large thru hike.

So I do just that. I play it safe. Though after everything is said and done I think I could definitely have done it as one big day. Going up the backside of Katahdin was fairly easy. I would say it is easier than what northbound hikers have to do on the side of the mountain I descended. The Knife’s Edge wasn’t too exposed save for one short saddle section where I had to descend and then climb back up a steep 40 feet. There was one easy rock climbing move to do that would have been disastrous if I fell. The whole time I traversed the Knife’s Edge it was a complete white out. Finally, I got to Katahdin, Baxter Peak. The start of the AT. I got my picture taken at the famous sign and ate some snacks up there, but even though it is only August it got pretty cold so after 30 minutes I decided to make my way down.

Unfortunately, it was still pretty foggy at the top of Baxter Peak.

Exactly one mile into the AT I turned off to start my side quest of Hamlin Peak. This was a two hour detour which involved going down and then up a saddle, summiting, and then going back down and up the saddle. Fun times. With that taken care of I continued my way down the mountain. There were a lot of sections with rebar drilled into the mountain as makeshift ladders. It was pretty steep. This is definitely the harder side. The sun attempted to come out at times, and by the time I made my way down the mountain it was actually a pretty nice day. I’ll have to come back sometime for better views from the top. I made it to Katahdin Stream Campground just in time to get a shuttle back to Millinocket.

The next day I shuttled back to where I left off except now I will have to try and hitch to the West side of Baxter State Park where North Brother resides. This side quest proved lengthy in time as I stood out there for an hour trying to hitch. Once I got picked up it was about a twenty minute drive. The actual hike was three hours round trip with another hour of trying to get a hitch and twenty minutes of driving back to Katahdin Stream Campground. With that six hour detour finished I continued along where I made it out of Baxter State Park to Abol Bridge Campground. Here I picked up a few items at the store and bought a very large ice cream cone. It was getting late so I hiked another three miles into the 100 Mile Wilderness and called it a night at the first shelter, Hurd Brook Lean-to. I’m not getting very far these first two days so I’m going to have to pick up the pace tomorrow.

I woke up fairly early the next day to get my miles in. I was on trail at 5:40am. The 100 Mile Wilderness is a famous section of the AT though I was surprised when I actually hiked it. Due to its name, it conjures up thoughts of pristine wilderness without any signs of civilization for miles and miles on end. While it might be true that you are far away from civilization, access to civilization and all of its allure still runs heavily through this section. There are some great hostels in the area that will slack pack you for a price. Slack packing is essentially when they hold onto your backpack and you hike your mileage for that day with just a day bag or just the essential gear. They will then pick you up at an agreed upon spot, and take you back to the hostel for a night of town food and a bed. There are many spots along the AT that do this, but here in the 100 Mile Wilderness it seems especially noticeable. There are even packages that can be purchased where you do this over ten days with a meal and bed every night. Such is the fame of the 100 mile wilderness that it brings in all types seeking to “conquer” it. Or at the very least be chauffeured through. Add onto this, there are many active logging roads to be crossed where logging trucks zoom by and the 100 Mile Wilderness is no longer the peaceful serene experience you might imagine. In fact, it is quite popular and crowded to the point where the mice have got in on the act. My first night’s campsite I had a visitor who chewed up a Butterfingers wrapper I had in a pocket. Fortunately, no damage was done to my pack, but this is fairly rare if you’re not staying at a shelter. I guess the campsite was too established.

Caution, unless of course, you want to pay for every luxury.

The 100 Mile Wilderness is beautiful. I can see why people flock to it even when they’re not doing the whole AT. While I did get a heavy taste of rain during my stay, the Maine wilderness is stunning. I’ve never backpacked in Maine before despite visiting many times. The forest is enchanted. There is moss and mushrooms everywhere. Many lakes dot the landscape. And I have arrived during blueberry season. I find at the top of every mountain there are more berries than I can pick. And I try. Believe me I try.

Another great place on the AT. I hope to be back someday.

They run a tight ship at Shaw’s. The owners, Hippie Chick and Poet, have everything down such that, upon being given the tour and asked if any questions, I am just left speechless as to how they distilled all the information I needed so clearly, concisely, and quickly. I was also given a free soda and ice cream sandwich upon arrival which was nice. One of the employees took me to the store later where I bought a very large pizza, jug of chocolate milk, and other goodies for resupply. I was very full. Shaw’s also has a gear store I perused with a nicely curated collection of backpacking gear including some more niche brands you cannot get online or through other big retailers. The one bummer is right before leaving I left my AT branded Darn Tough sleep socks somewhere in the room where I stayed, and by the time I realized and had service to call and see if they were still there several days later someone had swiped them. That was a darn tough pill to swallow as they were very new and those socks cost $28 as they have a lifetime warranty. You can’t really use that warranty without said socks in hand, however.

Famous stack of blueberry pancakes at Shaw’s.

The morning of leaving Shaw’s I had their famous breakfast before hitting trail again. Eggs, bacon, toast, and all you can eat blueberry pancakes. You will leave satisfied. I finish my last day of this week setting myself up for the Kennebec River crossing tomorrow. This is the only river along the AT wide enough that you must get ferried across. The Appalachian Trail Conservancy actually pays someone to ferry hikers across all day in season. The canoe even has a white blaze on it. After this it will truly be all hiking until Key West.

Maine has been such a treat to walk so far. I am excited for more enchanted forest.

In 2026 I will embark on my longest journey yet by walking from Newfoundland to Key West on the Eastern Continental Trail and completing my Triple Crown!

#8387. I Caught the World-Record Striped Bass During the Eclipse of a Full Moon

Published Oct 28, 2026 10:00 AM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

Somehow I knew that the full-moon night of July 16, 1981, was going to be special when I left my berth at Lake Montauk, New York, at the eastern extremity of Long Island. My only company on the 24-foot inboard-outboard was 13-year-old Eddie Turpek, who was on his first nighttime bass trip. We left at 9:30 p.m. My friend John Alberda and I had gotten word that a few big stripers had been trolled up the night before, and we felt sure that we could pick up a few fish by drifting live eels. John was fishing from his own boat, so we could cover all the likely areas and call each other on the radio if either of us hit fish.

The southwest breeze died after dark, and we were able to work our drifts perfectly at the end of the flood tide, but there was no action. However, I was marking bass on my recording depthfinder, and I was sure that they would turn on and feed sometime during the night.

It was a great night on the water. The sky was clear, and the full moon made it seem as bright as day until the eclipse started after midnight. The bass were still turned off at the beginning of the ebb. The waiting was too much for young Eddie, and he racked out in the small cabin.

Time after time I worked several spots I had fished for years. Then I tried several narrow ledges near the Great Eastern Buoy. Because bass have been getting scarcer, it has become ever more important to focus on tiny productive areas. Most of these ledges are in deeper water than we used to fish for bass. The drift usually starts over a 40-foot ledge that quickly slopes down to about a 50-foot depth. The big bass seem to hang in very specific slots where they can feed on baitfish coming over the ledge and still stay out of the full force of the moving tide.

When we first started this fishing, it was necessary to use visual ranges on buoys and objects ashore to locate a good area. Then we’d scout around the drop-off with the graph depth recorder and throw out a buoy if we marked fish on the paper. Today the miracle of Loran C has made it all a lot simpler. With the new pinpoint navigation gear, I can go back to an exact spot time after time, after which the graph recorder helps to pinpoint the proper drift for that particular stage of the tide and the wind velocity.

My tackle is simple. I use an Ambassadeur 8600 conventional reel. All the local bass experts favor reels of this type because the push-button release makes it easy to keep the terminal rig just above the bottom as the depth changes. All that’s required to put the reel back into gear is a flip of the reel handle. My rod is a custom-built job on an Ugly Stik blank. The reel had just been filled with some new 40-pound-test Ande blue mono that a friend had given me. My terminal rig consisted of a three-way swivel with a sinker (the size varies with the tide) attached on a short piece of mono, and a long leader to a 6/0 No. 92554 Mustad hollow-point hook. I’ve found that style to be ideal for this fishing. At one time I used stainless steel hooks, but I felt guilty because stainless steel hooks don’t rust out of bass that break off.

The eclipse was still going on at about 3:30 a.m. when my live eel got tapped. Usually big bass tap the eel first, and then it’s necessary to free-spool and drop back instantly so the bass can really grab the eel. I free-spooled and dropped back all right, but just as I got ready to set the hook, the bass bolted with the eel. The result was a massive backlash and a burnt thumb!

I was in big trouble, though I suspected that the fish was only a 30-pounder. The bass pulled out about 130 feet of line, right down to the knotty backlash. I couldn’t give any more line, so I walked forward from stern to bow using the bend in the rod to absorb the surges against the snarled mono. After a while I backed up and retrieved a few yards. By retrieving line this way several times I was able to get the fish within 20 feet of the boat. Then she (all trophy stripers are females) ran all the line out again, right down to the knots.

Once again I was able to stop her at the snarl and used the same procedure to get back some line. I realized now that I was dealing with a bass of respectable size, perhaps in the forties. Soon the fish was near the surface and swimming around the boat. Just as I was looking for my gaff she dived to the bottom with a great surge of power that brought me back to the backlash again. By that time I had the drag screwed down hard, but I couldn’t do anything with the fish. Perhaps, just perhaps, I thought, I’ve hooked a big fifty!

I kept turning the handle of the Ambassadeur, taking in an inch whenever it was available. I’d been fighting the fish for 10 minutes and was worried that the new rod (I’d previously used a somewhat stiffer blank) was too light. However, I worked the bass up again, and I had my four-foot aluminum-handled gaff in hand when the big cow bore down and stripped me right back to the knots again! Now I knew the fish had to be my first sixty. The only other possibility was that I had foul-hooked a medium-size bass in the body or tail. Never before had I experienced four such powerful runs against a stiff drag.

I applied maximum pressure again, and the fish rose on her own. She came up about 100 feet from the boat. I got my first real look at her finning in the moonlight. I reeled carefully, and she came in on her side. There was such a huge expanse of white showing that she didn’t even look like a bass! This was the chance I’d been working for, but when I hit her with the gaff, both rubber grips slipped off the handle and the gaff fell in the water!

The gaff’s hook was still in the fish. I grabbed the handle of the floating gaff, dropped my rod, and used both hands and my back to lift the fish into the boat. I’m six feet tall, weigh about 205 pounds, and pride myself on keeping in good condition, but it took everything I had to swing that fish aboard. As she came over the side I was knocked backward. After 15 minutes of playing her and about 600 yards of drifting, the fish was mine. She made one slap with her tail—a real boom—and she was through. I couldn’t even fit her in my 44-inch cooler. I finally realized that I had the sixty I’d yearned for!

Eddie Turpek was awake now and completely shocked by the size of the first live striper he’d ever seen. I called John Alberda on my CB radio and told him about the huge fish, but John urged me to go on fishing and catch another while they were still hitting. That’s exactly what I did, and on the next drift over the same spot Eddie’s first bass ever hit a 35-pounder. We missed a couple of others before going in at daylight for breakfast.

I was so nervous by that time that I was actually afraid to find out what the fish weighed. At Inlet Marina I showed my bass to veteran night striper charter skipper Frank Braddick, and he could only shake his head. Another night charter captain, Jack Passie, and John Alberda lifted the bass out of my boat with a boom used to unload commercial catches. At that point I had set my heart on 68 pounds, but I was afraid that I was too optimistic. The fish was weighed, and everyone on the dock shouted seventy-five pounds!

The next move was to take the fish to Montauk Marine Basin for weighing on a certified scale. Though I now have a wonderful job running a police patrol boat, I served my apprenticeship as a law-enforcement officer in the toughest areas of my county, and I was involved in many dangerous situations. But nothing shook me up more than the weighing of that bass. What if the Inlet Marina scales were off? Well, they were off, but in the right direction. The bass actually weighed 76 pounds. At 53 inches, the cow was relatively short for such great weight, but the 35½-inch girth made up for that.

Read Next: The Best Lures and Live Baits for Striped Bass

That’s the story of Bob Rocchetta’s fantastic catch in his own words as he told it to me shortly after he brought in the bass that will almost surely be the new all-tackle world-record striped bass. Though the International Game Fish Association hadn’t approved Bob Rocchetta’s record at the time this article went to press (August 1981), it is hard to imagine a refusal.

All of the tackle used in live-eel fishing complies with IGFA regulations, and there are plenty of witnesses to the legitimacy of the catch. Obviously, in this case, identification of the species is not in doubt. Most legitimate catches on sporting tackle are accepted by IGFA if the fish is fought by a single angler. If you’re interested in the rules and procedures, write to IGFA, 3000 East Las Olas Boulevard, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33316.

In 1913 an angler named C. B. Church trolled a 73-pound striped bass up from the hallowed bassing grounds in Vineyard Sound, Massachusetts, to establish an all-tackle record that has been recognized by striper fishermen ever since. To be sure, the IGFA withdrew recognition of Church’s catch in recent years during one of its periodic reviews of records. The reason was that Church’s claim had never been properly documented in accordance with current IGFA procedures. Nevertheless, that’s the record that every striper angler had been shooting at. Until July 17, they all failed.

Actually, there have been a few close calls over the years. The 73-pound record was tied during the 60s by Charlie Cinto while fishing on Capt. Frank Sabatowski’s charterboat off Cuttyhunk Island, Massachusetts. However, the IGFA didn’t recognize that fish because it was caught on wire line and hit a big plug bristling with treble hooks. Then, on October 10, 1969, Edward J. Kirker boated a 72-pounder on an eel at Cuttyhunk, a catch that received official IGFA recognition as the all-tackle and 50-pound-test class world records.

Considering that striped bass in the 60-pound class are caught every year, it’s hard to believe that the popularly accepted 73-pound record endured so long. In addition to the saltwater fisheries on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, stripers are now thriving in fresh water, and there is a real possibility that a landlocked striper may one day top all the records. As it is, the National Fresh Water Hall of Fame currently recognizes a 59-pound 12-ounce bass taken from the Colorado River in Arizona as the landlocked record.

Breaking a record set in 1913 is a remarkable feat, but that’s no reason to think that it can’t be broken again. Very big fish seem to run in cycles and are often particularly abundant as the species declines. No one caught a bluefin tuna weighing 1,000 pounds until 1970. Now quite a few well over that mark are caught every year, though the species is in big trouble. Certainly the Atlantic coastal run of striped bass is in bad shape, but trophy fish seem more abundant than ever—possibly because of lessened competition for food. There are records of stripers that weighed up to 125 pounds caught by commercial fishermen.

To striper enthusiasts, it’s a pleasure to know that the new record fish was caught by an experienced, very skilled fisherman and not by someone who relied on a charterboat captain and mate to do most of the thinking and work. Bob Rocchetta, now 32 years old, caught his first striper in the Narrows area of Conscience Bay, Long Island, when he was 13 years old. Bob had to learn the ropes from old-timers and many magazine articles and books. After graduating from college, he went to work for the Suffolk County police department, and he bought a four-wheel-drive vehicle so that he could surf cast at Montauk. He had to learn that art from scratch but did quite well with bass and bluefish by casting live eels. However, watching boats working areas well beyond his reach, Bob decided that he’d never be satisfied without a boat of his own.

Just as he was getting into a financial position to buy a decent boat, Bob got married, and instead of a boat he had to invest in a home. Nevertheless, he found an old garvey and rebuilt it and an old engine for a total investment of about $250.

To become a better fisherman Bob knew that he needed a bigger boat. He was eyeing one at a local boat dealer’s but couldn’t justify spending the family’s money on it. Then the engine in the old garvey seized up, and it looked as if he’d be beached for quite a while. Returning home dejected, Bob was met by his wife who told him that she’d just made a down payment on the boat with money she’d saved from her own salary.

The boat was soon in the water, and the fisherman was free to expand his horizons until he finally hit the giant cow bass off Great Eastern Rock during an eclipse of the moon.

This story was originally published in the November 1981 issue of Outdoor Life.
