#8366. The Best Rifle Scopes for Deer Hunting, Tested & Reviewed

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:04 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I grew up deer hunting in the woods of north-central Wisconsin where a 100-yard shot would be a long one. We needed only a simple 3-9X riflescope that gathered enough light to let us shoot a half-hour after sunset. In other words, any streamlined riflescope with decent glass would work just fine.

A lot of deer hunters still hunt this same way. But riflescope offerings have grown exponentially. So the best riflescope for deer hunting really depends on where, and how, you intend to hunt.

With this roster of scopes I’ve attempted to select a good variety of styles that will work in the northwoods, the open country of the West, and everywhere in between. All of my picks are based on data from in-depth testing conducted by OL’s Optics Editor Andrew McKean and our Gear Editor Scott Einsmann. I focus mostly on affordable options, but there are a couple high-end picks included, too.

The Burris Fullfield is a classic deer scope, built on a 1-inch tube with capped turrets and a second-plane duplex reticle. It’s a simple, capable scope that’s offered for under $300.

​This scope has some nice features, including distinctive red accents on the power-changing ring and turret dials and re-zeroable turrets. But it’s not perfect either. It has a distracting greenish coating that’s especially noticeable in low-light conditions. Its turret indexing is so tiny that it’s hard to confirm when you’re zeroed.

But for a good image, plus simple and repeatable controls, the Burris Fullfield 3-12×42 checks every box for the workaday deer hunter.

Nightforce is known for building battle-ready riflescopes for long-range precision shooting. But their new NX6 product line is designed specifically for hunters. I used the 3-18X50 F1 version with a MIL reticle on an elk hunt this fall and found it to be an excellent open-country hunting scope. It had strong image quality and low-light performance. It’s a hefty scope, but not absurdly so, like some other precision optics.

One of the key features of the NX6 line is the new FieldSet turret system. Once you’ve established your zero, any simple tool — a coin, knife, or flat rock — will loosen the exposed turret cap, allowing you to reset your zero and set the zero stop. The stop can be set a full revolution above zero, or 2 MILs.

One of the many cool things about this system is that any NX6 model except the 1-6x can be converted from capped to exposed turret, and the standard exposed turret can be traded for a custom BDC turret. It’s another indication that the NX6 is positioned to be the ultimate versatile scope family.

The scope comes with a versatile illumination system that lights up the entire reticle. This is a relatively advanced and expensive scope, but for spun-up riflemen who are looking to shoot deer at longer ranges, it’s an excellent option.

The latest incarnation of Trijicon’s legendary AccuPoint line, this durable LPVO is designed to withstand the recoil of big-bucking magnums. Its always-on illumination doesn’t require a battery to fire. Its balance, style, and grit befit a bespoke rifle that’s imagined as an heirloom but used as your ride-or-die hunting gun.

Instead of relying on a battery, the Trijicon’s illumination is activated by sunlight that hits the windows of a fiber-optic receptor and translates photons into intensity of a fine 0.25 MOA green dot at the intersection of a bold second focal-plane duplex reticle. In low-light situations, the element tritium does the work of the sun and supplies the energy to light up that aiming point.

It’s an elegant and durable system that’s optimized for this 1-8×24 build, which neatly fits every AR and straight-wall cartridge carbine made. The scope’s Dangerous Game BDC reticle in MOA is built for close-in and medium-range target work. The tough detail is its price, which is steep.

The excellent glass, tight but understated controls and tasteful lines elevate the Trijicon to a level of sophistication that most grubby LPVOs can’t reach.

The TANGO-MSR Compact brings plenty of versatility in a package that measures 8.4 inches and comes pre-mounted on a very good cantilever unimount for the screaming price of $399.

The glass in this scope isn’t great, but everything else about this little marvel is spot-on. The second-plane arrangement in the TANGO-MSR is simple and useful. The inverted-horseshoe center aiming arrangement blazes bright in daylight conditions, and the BDC grid is useful for placing bullets with precision on targets out to 500 yards. The only real tradeoff is that the scope must be set at its highest magnification for the bullet-drop subtensions to be accurate.

We put the scope through a battery of close-range fast-fire drills, and atop an AR carbine, then we slowed things down and rang steel out to a quarter-mile with the scope. It performed admirably in all cases.

The TANGO-MSR is optimized for AR, but it would be great on a straight-wall cartridge carbine or muzzleloader.

The Crossfire HD line, slowly replacing the Crossfire 2 line, has a scope for every hunter, from a handy LPVO to a big 6-18×50 model to this mid-mag optic that’s optimized for America’s deer hunters.

The 4-12×44 model is priced at only $300, and is an excellent budget option. It’s built on the second focal-plane arrangement and with MOA-based aiming points. There’s the classic Dead-Hold BDC that’s a non-illuminated plex design with three bullet-drop references and windage hashed. Or you can opt for an illuminated version of that reticle, with a pin-point illuminated center dot for a $50 upcharge. Or you can go old-school and use the Widerange Plex, which is basically a German #4 duplex without illumination.

The glass in the Crossfire HD line didn’t blow us away, but the magnification range is right in the sweet spot for whitetail hunters, and we found it to be an easy, simple, and budget workhorse.

“I think your average hunter would take this over the other $300 scopes in our test. It’s worth that price all day long,” noted Outdoor Life optics tester Todd Netto.

For $450, you get some great features and performance from the V3. It is offered in three versions of its second-plane reticle build, a non-illuminated No. 6 plex and both non-illuminated and center-dot illuminated versions of the SHR (it stands for Smart Hunting Reticle) hash-style design with MOA-based holdover and windage references. The illuminated version has a crisp center dot that shines with a red illumination.

These new Zeiss scopes are no longer made in Europe. They’re sourced in Asia, but if that suggests a decline in optical performance or brand integrity, worry not. These are excellent scopes that use premium components. Also, they’re designed for the American hunter.

For a price-point scope, Bushnell’s R5 has some surprisingly sophisticated features. The most useful is its second focal-plane DOA-LRH800 reticle.

The modified tree-style reticle is extremely tunable, meaning that for shooters and hunters willing to invest the time, the Bushnell Ballistics app can produce customized drop tables for your specific load and magnification setting. Not too shabby for a $250 scope.

The R5 doesn’t have quite the smooth and confident controls of its big sibling, the R7 introduced earlier this year, but it’s a more responsive and precise build than most scopes in its price range. If you’re willing to spend a little more, consider the R7 line which won our 2026 Editor’s Choice award for best all-around hunting scope.

This is a throwback deer scope in all the best ways. It’s hardy and durable. It’s simple and reliable.

The Maven brings a second focal-plane MOA-based reticle that’s clean and easy to see. The heart of the scope is the wire-frame CSHR-W reticle, which provides 20 MOA of windage references on the horizontal stadia at 10x, along with 20 MOA of elevation holdover. At $425, the Maven is priced in a sweet spot for deer hunters.

Sometimes you just need a simple, old-school optic for your deer gun. This stripped-down fixed-power scope from Athlon is designed for muzzleloaders, but it could just as easily work on a lever gun.

There’s remarkably little to say about this Talos HMR. Its 1x magnification is pretty solid, without the fishbowl distortion of some low-power scopes. The duplex reticle is proven. There are no illumination or parallax controls to worry about.

All that simplicity holds the Athlon back, of course. It’s not going to help you reach out beyond 300 yards to ring a steel target, and it’s not going to offer any windage or hold-over marks. But it should be durable and fast to target at shots at deer inside 100 yards.

Leupold is filling out its product line with this 4-times zoom ratio family that bridges the gap between the VX-3HD and the VX-5HD. Significantly, the VX-4HD scopes feature Leupold’s excellent push-button 2-revolution CDS-ZL2 elevation dials, and not the toolless Gen2 turrets that it’s rolling out with its other premium scope lines.

You’ll recognize many of the features of the VX-4HD line. It’s built on a second focal-plane system with a fairly standard selection of reticles: duplex, Wind-Plex with 1 MOA hashes extending to 10 MOA on either side of the center crosshair, and illuminated FireDot Twilight Hunter.

​But the new family has upgraded optics, delivering a bright, crisp, and vibrant image. An important point for deer hunters: the 4-20×50 won our low-light test, thanks to the big 50mm objective lens and the excellent glass and coatings. Its removeable elevation turret can be traded out for a free custom ballistic dial tuned to your own bullet and load (second CDS dials cost $80). The scope itself costs about $1,000, with illumination adding another $100 to $200, depending on configuration.

Sure there might be brighter, more powerful, and more feature-rich scopes on the market. But those optics aren’t what most deer hunters want, or need. The best deer scope is functional, reliable, and simple. Hopefully, it’s affordable too. So that’s how we built this list of scopes. For more detailed coverage on how we conduct our riflescope testing, check out our reviews on the best LPVOs, Best Hunting Scopes, and Best Precision Rifle Scopes.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8365. One Dead, Two Injured as Two Helicopters Crash Near Everest Base Camp

An Indian passenger died and two more were injured when two helicopters crashed while landing near Everest Base Camp this morning.

The helicopters were operated by Fishtail Air and Air Dynasty, two of Nepal’s largest companies. The crash occurred at the helipad on the outskirts of the village of Pheriche (4,371m). It’s a typical spot for helicopters to stop and refuel when on their way to and from Everest Base Camp.

As shown in the horrific video below, the two helicopters came from different directions, and both tried to land at the same time. Somehow their rotor blades collided. The inexplicable crash occurred in a wide, flat area with good visibility.

Vasanth Kumar, an Indian trekker, died on the spot, The Tourism Times reported. Shailesh Kishan from New Zealand and Rabindra Prajapati, a senior captain, were seriously injured. Both have been airlifted to hospitals in Kathmandu. They were all on board the Fishtail Air helicopter. The Air Dynasty chopper was carrying cargo.

#8362. New Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding new route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

They placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health issues. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The new line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

Attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

This was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov

#8361. Grumpylocks and the Three Bears

The Ice Age Trail’s camping options are a little more restrictive than you might expect. Even the western region has plenty of segments where you can’t simply hit your miles for the day and just find the nearest flat spot. Here’s where I spent my nights on the IAT.

While some trailheads on the IAT had “No Overnight Parking/Camping” signs, the four where I stayed did not. Just four days into my hike, I camped at a trailhead next to a quiet dirt road where traffic wasn’t the reason I kept waking up. Heat, humidity, and stagnant air were the problem.

There was still no hint of a breeze by morning, and I was sweating before I left camp. I was filtering water at the next trailhead when a pair of day-hikers arrived. They parked their car, hit the trail, and it was probably half an hour before I caught up with them. They smelled nice and clean: a scent I picked up at least a minute before I saw them again. That’s how still the air was. I’m sure I smelled fine.

That morning’s trail was lined with some sort of tall grass which was shedding tiny disk-like seeds that stuck to my sweaty skin. By the time I reached the road to Haugen, my arms and legs had the texture of 60 grit sandpaper.

The three miles of blacktop between me and my intended destination were hot: probably the most uncomfortable of the entire trail. The Shady Rest Campground was about an hour away, and I was looking forward to a cool shower and a cold drink. FarOut comments even mentioned that they have air-conditioned cabins. When I arrived, the office was closed. It was a Monday.

Fortunately, one of the owner’s friends was nearby. She called the owner, who rented me a cabin. She also gave me a ride into town and some quarters for the shower. Again, I’m sure I smelled fine.

At Lona’s Corner Cafe, I sat as far as possible from the other customers. I discovered a tick on my arm during lunch. As casually and covertly as possible, I removed the tick using the array of utensils in front of me, making sure it would never bite anyone else.

After a quick stop at the grocery store for five days’ worth of food, I walked back to the campground to take a shower. Once I’d completed my chores, I literally chilled in my cabin for the rest of the afternoon.

I visited the store again on my way out of town the next morning. After breakfast on the bench across the street, I headed south on the Wild Rivers State Trail, then east on the Tuscobia State Trail. Both trails are wide (former railroads) but I was still a little surprised to be overtaken by a horse and buggy. At the end of the day, with no better options, I stopped at another trailhead.

The mosquitoes were hungry the following morning. I was carrying a small bottle of DEET for emergency use, but I wasn’t sure the situation qualified. I’d encountered worse. Still, after eight itchy miles, I wanted a break. I left the trail at the north end of Stout Road and enjoyed an hour of bug-free bliss. Even the hound that bounded beyond its house’s boundary to hound me wasn’t really a problem, despite its loud, raspy bark. It was never going to bite. It was, as they say, “All mouth and no trousers.”

I know some people hike every inch of official trail, but I need flexibility during a thru-hike. This wouldn’t be the last time I deviated from the trail, and in the end, my way was no more arbitrary than the IAT itself. The Blue Hills segments I hiked that day have since been re-routed, reducing the number of official trail miles.

This was to be my first of many days that were more road than trail. No surprise, the air was still and the mosquitoes voracious. I used some of my precious DEET to shield me while I broke camp and hiked 2.6 miles. For most of that distance, the trail crossed private land, and I could smell the cows long before I saw them. After an hour, I started a road-walk that would last all day.

At the gas station in Weyerhaeuser, I topped-up on fuel and coolant. On the other side of town, I spotted an animal that I initially thought was a large dog. I’d never seen such a lean, long-legged bear. She saw me and hurried across the road with two cubs close behind.

Eventually, the scenery started to change. Isolated farms were replaced with frequent lakeside houses. Having covered 21 miles by 1 PM, I stopped for a break at Round Lake County Park. I was way ahead of schedule, just three miles from the DCA were I intended to camp.

The IAT passes plenty of state, county, and city parks, each of which is a gift when you’re a thru-hiker. They typically have water, picnic tables, a pavilion, electrical outlets, trash cans, and pit (sometimes flush) toilets. Round Lake was my first county park on the IAT. I spent three hours at a picnic table in the pavilion, and used all the amenities. I also spoke to Paul and Cindy, the first of many hikers I’d meet who were hiking the entire IAT, one piece at a time. They offered to leave a beer for me at a local bar, and I eagerly accepted. This was a trail-magic first.

I hung out until four, went for a swim, rinsed my clothes, and wrung them out. They were almost dry by the time I arrived at The King’s Inn, two miles later. Paul and Cindy had indeed bought me a beer. I had three more with dinner, then walked one more mile to my campsite. Not a typical day, but an enjoyable one.

The morning was cool and overcast, and a light rain started at midday. A runner training for a 50k overtook me, slowing for a few minutes to chat before continuing his out-and-back. For the next 90 minutes, the rain just kept getting heavier. Eventually, on a wide section of trail, I put up my tent in “shelter” mode: footprint and rainfly only. I’d applied seam-sealant before my hike, but I discovered that the fly still leaked. The runner, Jacob, returned 45 minutes later. There was enough room in my makeshift shelter for two, even if it was a little cramped. We went our separate ways an hour after that, once the rain began to ease. It was still sprinkling when I reached my DCA an hour later, but a mylar heat-sheet beneath the leaky fly successfully redirected the drips.

Before leaving Chippewa County for Taylor County, I had a decision to make. If I spent two or three days on the IAT, I’d hike more than 40 miles of road and only half a mile of trail.

If I made my own way, I’d hike 25 miles of busy state highway and zero miles of trail. I chose option one.

I arrived in Cornell just after 9 AM, and the mayor pulled over to chat as I was walking down Main Street. After breakfast at Sam’s Place, I bought a five day resupply and hit the road at 11 o’clock. I stopped at Hidden Shady Nook campground mid-afternoon. The bartender introduced me to Spotted Cow beer, and I enjoyed a few air-conditioned hours overlooking Pike Lake.

The next day, Sunday, was even shorter. I left at 7 AM, and reached the south end of Otter Lake in less than four hours. The boat ramp was busy and the parking lot was half full. I ate some snacks while filtering water, walked a quarter mile back to the trailhead, and 0.6 trail miles to the DCA. The day was warm, with no rain in the forecast, so I didn’t bother with the rain fly. I put up my tent in the shade of an impressive tree, and settled down to read.

An hour later, although I didn’t hear anyone approach, I heard a voice say flatly, “Oh.” I raised my head just in time to see a guy turn around and leave. He was dressed more like a golfer than a hiker, and he wasn’t carrying anything. I guessed he was scouting the campsite before bringing gear and/or people.

At 4:30 PM, I had another visitor. This one wasn’t using the trail, and made no effort to hide its approach through dead leaves and dry brush. I raised my head again, and turned awkwardly to my right. An adult black bear. Realization took a second, but during that second, she continued to move deliberately, directly towards me.

“THAT’S CLOSE ENOUGH!” I was nearly at full volume.

She stopped immediately, calmly, almost casually. She avoided looking in my direction, but stayed where she was, about 20 yards away. Then, almost in unison, two furry little faces popped up out of the brush next to her. It was the cubs’ turn to take a moment. While they gathered their thoughts, I sat bolt upright. The nearest cub sprinted in my general direction.

Fortunately, the cub hadn’t been overcome by curiosity. It wasn’t helpless to resist the aroma of dried apricots coming from my bear canister. It had simply decided that, without checking for any alternatives, there was only one suitable tree in the vicinity. That tree was about 10 yards from my tent, a yard or two off the direct line of sight between me and its mother.

The sound of claws on tree-bark was surprisingly loud. Also, that little bear could climb surprisingly quickly. The second cub was close behind, just as quick, and climbed just as loudly. They went high enough that I couldn’t see or hear them.

Momma bear didn’t react when the cubs’ instincts/training kicked in. I didn’t see any change in her body language. She wasn’t aggressive, agitated, or even concerned. She just stood there, on all fours, shuffling a little from left to right, looking anywhere but at me.

They all needed some space, I decided. I narrated what I was doing as I unzipped my tent, put on my flipflops, and zipped up the door. I continued talking as I unscrewed the lid of my bear can, stuffed my toiletries into it, and screwed the lid back down. Click. Click. There wasn’t enough space in the canister for my evening meal, so I took it with me.

Armed with two blocks of ramen, I retreated down a short spur trail marked by little yellow flags. After about 20 yards, I shut the f*ck up, turned around, and waited. I was close enough to intervene if the bear went for my stuff, but far enough that the cubs would come down from the tree. That was the plan, anyway.

Momma was no longer interested in the canister, or any of my gear. It took her about 30 minutes to shuffle slowly, hesitantly to the base of the tree. She stood on her hind legs, front paws against the trunk, looking up, trying to coax the cubs down. I couldn’t see or hear any movement from above. All I could hear were Momma’s gentle calls, repeated every minute or two. Each call sounded like a sigh mixed with a groan, followed by three short exhalations through pursed lips. It was interesting, but ineffective. The cubs weren’t coming down.

By now, I’d accumulated 45 minutes’ worth of mosquito bites, and I’d run out of patience. I turned my narration back on and flipflopped back to my tent.

Breaking camp took about 15 minutes – a new personal record. I bundled everything haphazardly into my pack while giving a grumpy commentary. Mom, meanwhile, was still giving words of encouragement to the cubs.

I didn’t see the bears again, despite spending the night at the boat-ramp parking lot, only a quarter mile from the DCA as the crow flies.

This wasn’t a habituated bear, it was a food-conditioned bear. I don’t think she just happened to pick up the scent of my bear canister. With only one exception, all black bears I’ve previously encountered have been quick to show me their big jiggly ass when they ran away. This bear was brazen enough to come into camp in broad daylight, so even if she’d run away, she was probably coming back at night. The cubs did a fine job of distracting her from her mission.

I wonder how many times golfer-guy had hiked to the DCA only to find it occupied? Enough to justify a 1.2 mile round trip, apparently. Surely there can’t be that many IAT hikers using the DCA. And even if IAT hikers were always camping there, they probably know how to store their food properly. It seems likely that the DCA is frequented by non-outdoorsy types who don’t know that “A fed bear is a dead bear.”

At the very least, a fed bear is a f*cking nuisance. Its cubs might grow up to be just as much of a problem. I’m probably preaching to the choir when I tell you to store your pic-a-nic baskets properly.

I added a FarOut comment about the bear, and submitted a trail alert on the IATA website. I used a little less detail for those though.

Wisconsin road users (that snake’s fake, btw).

#8359. “I Was in Disbelief.” Crossbow Hunter Takes Massive 250-Class, 290-Pound Nontypical Buck

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:40 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Mike Ferriman, a 42-year-old agricultural sales rep from Caledonia, Ohio first learned of a giant buck this year on a farm he has permission to hunt on September 22. A few trail camera photos revealed that the massive whitetail’s rack was similar to a heavy buck he had photos of last year on the same farm.

“But this year his rack had just blown up,” Ferriman tells Outdoor Life. “There were some familiar kicker points to the rack, but it was a lot bigger and heavier.”

Ferriman didn’t have many trail cam pictures of the deer before he got into a 21-foot-high ladder stand on the farm in heavy timber the afternoon of October 20.

“I had a mineral site set up in the woods 30 yards from my ladder stand, with a couple trail cameras nearby,” says Ferriman. “The big buck came through the area the night of Oct. 18, and I got one photo of him, and he was gone.

“The next night on Oct. 19 he came to the mineral site at 6 p.m., and he hung around awhile. The buck checked the same mineral spot three times that night, so I knew I had to hunt the stand the next evening provided I had a good northeast wind.”

Fortunately, the wind was perfect, and the crossbow hunter walked to his stand that following afternoon.

“I bumped a couple does walking 300 yards to the stand, but the place is full of deer and no matter how or when I go in I move some deer,” he says. “I got up in my stand, and pretty soon I was surrounded by about a dozen does.

“They were very close, and I’m convinced they didn’t catch my scent because of the Ozonics scent control I was using. It was 70 degrees and I was sweating a lot. But no deer scented me.”

That evening was only the second time Ferriman had hunted the spot, and he knew another heavy buck was in the vicinity, too.

“I had two big bucks in the area – I’m just glad the biggest one showed up first,  so I didn’t have to decide whether to take the smaller one, which was still a giant deer,” he says.

With does everywhere around his ladder stand, Ferriman noticed movement on a trail and quickly realized the huge non-typical buck was headed toward his mineral site.

“He came straight in toward me from 90 yards away where I first spotted him,” he says. “I almost took a shot at him at 50 yards, but he kept coming and a closer shot was what I wanted.

“He went behind a downed tree and some brush and just stood there. Then he stepped out, head down, but was facing me. I thought about a neck shot when he looked up. But just then a doe behind me made a noise, and he turned quartering away, and I took my shot at 30 yards.”

Using a Ravin crossbow, his Rage Hypodermic 2-blade, 100-grain arrow penetrated completely through the buck.

“I heard a loud thud from the arrow hitting and watched him run – and almost in slow motion – he went 50 yards and fell,” Ferriman recalls. “I was in disbelief and couldn’t comprehend how fast he’d piled up.”

Ferriman used binoculars to check the downed buck, and confirmed the giant deer was down for good.

He sent out text messages to his wife Holly and some friends alerting them of his success, and requesting help to get the deer out.

Shortly, Holly and his pals arrived and used a drag sled to get the huge buck out of the woods and into a truck. They went to a friend’s house, where they had a scale that could weigh the massive deer.

Ferriman says the deer weighed 290 pounds, not field dressed.

He took the buck to Toby Hughes, a Buckmasters official scorer in Ohio, who measured the rack’s 28 scorable points at 250 3/8s inches.

The deer is estimated at 5.5 to 6.5 years old, and its teeth will be officially aged, just as Ferriman does with all his bucks.

Read Next: Ohio Farmer Tags 231-Inch ‘Flyer’ Buck That He Missed Two Years Ago

Ferriman is a schooled taxidermist and will have the deer mounted, perhaps even a full-body mount.

“I’ve shot some great deer, some up to 150-inches,” he says. “But this buck is far and away the best I’ve ever taken.”

#8358. Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

This won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this important riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8355. Forester Pass, Through the Notch — John Muir Trail Day 5

A truly scary thing happened in the middle of last night.  I lay in my sleeping bag and suddenly realized I couldn’t remember the name of the highest mountain in the Lower 48.  Yes, the one I had climbed myself just two days previously.  I mean, I couldn’t think of it AT ALL.

I thought, “Ummmm… Mount McKinley, that’s in Alaska.  Mount Mansfield, that’s in Vermont.  Mount…”   I came up with Mount Whittier and I thought, “Maybe that’s it, Whittier.  Is it?”  It didn’t really sound right, but I honestly couldn’t think of the name.  I groped for it, but it just would not come to me.

Finally, I fell back to sleep and then, as I woke up, it gradually came to me.  “Oh, Whitney, yeah, Whitney, yes, Mount Whitney!”  But what was going on?  Was I getting  Alzheimer’s?  As I said, it was a very scary thing.

I also spent a couple of hours of my allotted sleeping time thinking about my sisters.  Sam urged that I find forgiveness.  I thought maybe I could write to them and say, “Look, I have a deep well of sadness and disappointment at how this has played out.  Yes, and anger too.”

“But there is also a well of forgiveness in me waiting to be awakened.  At some point in the future, in the near or far future, you may consider the possibility that you were not completely fair to your brother.  A little doubt may creep in about whether you honored your sibling relationship in a truly loving and caring way.  If that day ever comes, remember that well of forgiveness remains in my heart.”

Alas, the result of all that tossing and turning was that eight hours of sleep was actually four hours of real sleep.

Then the alarm went off, right at 4:30.  We wanted to get up early to go over Forester Pass.  At 13,153 feet elevation, it is the highest point on the Pacific Crest Trail and the highest pass on the John Muir Trail.  We wanted to get across before the weather changed.

The tendency had been for good weather in the morning and then, by late morning or early afternoon, the clouds built up, and the weather got stormy.

When the alarm went off, I felt like I hadn’t slept much at all.  Also, I was still coughing.  So I was not moving very quickly.

One brilliant move I made was to set up for breakfast in my sleeping bag.  For the first time on trail, it got cold during the night.  When I went out to pee, I thought it might be nearly morning and I moved my bear cannister close to my tent flap.

Back within the tent, I wondered whether I ought to insert my silk liner inside the sleeping bag for the first time.  I decided if it was nearly 4:30 I would not bother.  But the Garmin showed it was barely 12:30 – half past midnight!  Facing four more hours of attempted sleep in the cold I got out the silk liner.

Oh, my goodness, the sleeping bag liner makes such a difference!  It’s just wonderful, the difference between chilly and toasty.  It weighs almost nothing too; definitely one of my favorite hiking luxuries.

After the alarm, I had my “breakfast in bed.”  Then I lay in my sleeping bag for a while letting my digestion settle before going out to poop.  Less than ten minutes later I had assembled my tools and was facing the cathole I had so cleverly dug the night before.  All well there, I returned to my campsite and began to break it down and pack.

I was slow.  I don’t know why, because my pack was getting smaller with less food in it.  It should have been easier and faster.  In any case, our planned 5:30 departure turned out to be closer to 6:30, but still earlier than most of the campers in our vicinity.

We were on our way to Forester Pass.  I worried that it might actually be harder to tackle than Mount Whitney because we would cross with our full packs, not the lighter version we had carried to the summit.  As we left camp, the first thing we discovered was a sign indicating the pass was not four miles distant but five.

But it was a glorious morning, so beautiful.  Soon after our departure, the sun rose and the skies were blue; the glow shone across the mountains, across the boulder-strewn hillsides.

We cast long shadows in the early morning!

We even discovered a little early morning company!

How does Mr. Rabbit know that I am not a predator?

We ran into a guy named Marty, a carpenter from Salt Lake City.  He had decided that being a carpenter alone was not going to provide him with income in his old age.  So, he began buying dilapidated houses and fixing them up.  He then turned them into rentals.

Sam sensed the possibility of a political dispute.  He interjected diplomatically that it was time we kept moving.  Still, we walked with Marty for quite a long time as we gradually made our way up the valley, higher and higher, closer and closer to Forester Pass.

Along the way we met another hiker, Lauralyn.  She and her husband Doug own the Mt Williamson Motel and Basecamp, a lodging in Independence, CA famous among hikers in the High Sierras.  I wondered whether Sam and I might stay there a night when we got off trail.  She encouraged us.

Lauralyn seemed really nice. She was also inspirational.  She was no longer young and skinny, but her enthusiasm for hiking the High Sierra was unabated.  Her pace may have slowed, but her vigor and sunny disposition still glowed.  I really hoped we would stay at her motel, and I volunteered to recite The Raven for the owners and guests if we stayed there.

Meeting her brought home that Sam and I were just a couple of days away from going off trail at Onion Valley.  I asked her where the best steak was in the vicinity and she told us to go to The Seasons restaurant in Lone Pine.  I was salivating already.

Salivating, yes, but coughing too.  I was still coughing so much.  Blowing my nose frequently or hawking up big globs of mucus from my lungs.  It was disgusting and demoralizing.  Since starting out, I had better days and worse days, but overall, I had not felt healthy and well at all.  This respiratory infection just felt endless.

As we grew nearer, Marty pointed out a low-lying ridge that he thought was Forester Pass.  I disagreed, suggesting it might be a notch on a different ridgeline. As we got closer it became clear that it was the tiny, narrow notch.  The approach is a slow and steady uphill until the base of the mountain, when it becomes an almost vertical face.

The “notch” seen from below. If you look closely, you can see the outline of the trail passing just below the giant boulder filling the notch.

There was a stream at the base and Marty went on alone as Sam and I stopped to replenish our water.  The ascent is basically into a rock wall.  In 1930 they cut zigzag switchbacks going up the side of the cliff face.  It was a big engineering feat. At one point, a young man died in the process of making it.

Donald Downs was only 18 years old. He was a few weeks shy of his 19th birthday when he died, and his fellow workers created a plaque and left it there in his honor.

Photo courtesy of Lawrence Beck (since I forgot to capture it when I passed by)

I was amazed to have the energy to hike, especially as we began to steadily climb.  It was a little past 10:00 a.m. and our theory about “good weather in the morning” was about to take a hit.

It is astonishing, in the mountains, how fast the clouds can come in.  Suddenly, as we hiked upwards, we got pelted with graupel.  Those little pellets – neither snow nor ice — are not hard enough to be hail and not wind-driven enough to be sleet, not flaky enough to be snow, nor wet enough to be rain.  In a way, if we had to face precipitation, this was perfect because they hit us softly and then bounced off of us.  Neither of us really needed rain gear because it wasn’t accumulating on us.  On the other hand, it was not easing up either.

Not the best shot of it, but you can see the graupel landing and sitting on the plant’s leaves.

Finally, we reached the notch we had seen from afar and climbed the last rocky ascent to Forester Pass.  The moment was triumphant but short-lived, since the weather was bad and the thunder was thundering.

Sam said, “Let’s keep going,” and we did.  On the other side of the pass was a long, long, long downhill.

It began with switchbacks at first, all well above the tree line.  At that altitude the rocks are plainly visible and, as I frequently did on the trip, I asked Sam to explain the geology to me.  He studied the subject in college and made a career in it.  For my part, I am curious about everything and glad when I find a passionate expert who seems to welcome my questions.

We would look at a slab of granite, for example, and Sam would explain that granite is made of mica, quartz, and feldspar in varying proportions.  He got especially excited when we encountered crystal inclusions in the rock, which he termed phenocrysts.  In fact, I suggested that his trail name should be “Phenocryst,” though I am not sure it stuck.

When the conversation turned back to my sisters, I saw Sam get visibly annoyed for the first and only time.  He was talking about the Dalai Lama’s book, The Wisdom of Forgiveness.  In it, the Dalai Lama apparently discusses forgiving the Chinese for their atrocious behavior in overrunning Tibet.

I could not resist commenting that if there was any analogy with my sisters, then, seeing how little success the Tibetans have had in changing Chinese hearts and minds, maybe the lesson is that I should just give up on my sisters.  Sam clearly did not appreciate my flip remark.  He has such an even temper that I was astonished by his reaction and immediately apologized.

As we conversed and descended the graupel turned to snow for a little while and then to rain.  We passed some patches of snow left from the winter.

This was not the first snow we saw, but given our elevation I was surprised not to see more than we did.

We concluded the rain was not a passing shower, and I finally put on my rain poncho, and Sam donned his rain gear.

It wasn’t truly miserable, but it was not very pleasant hiking in the rain.  The next day we were going off trail at Onion Valley, where Sam’s rental car was parked, so we wanted to reach Vidette Meadow to ensure a moderate distance the following day.

As we hiked, we watched the weather changing in the mountains.  It is so unpredictable, because you cannot see what is just over the nearest ridge.  At times it felt like we were about to get clear skies, then it felt like the heavens were going to burst open in a thunderous flood.  In fact, it did neither, it just rained and rained as we descended.

Vidette Meadow was a large area with many potential campsites.  We checked out about ten of them, seeking a couple that were not too wet and soggy from the rain.  At last Sam found two fairly close together.  One was a very dicey spot right under a tree, but Sam said he wanted it.  Who was I to say no?

I took the other site which was wetter, but larger and flatter, and we set up.  It was still dripping rain when we started and then it came down a little harder while we were making camp.  So it was not terrible, but not so nice.  I was really tired.

Approving my campsite, with a little hill behind me…

It was a long day. Basically, I moved everything I owned into the tent. When the weather is nice, I leave a lot of my gear outside. But I thought, with the rain, let me just bring it all in.

I cold-soaked a beef stew, my last dinner before resupply.  Then I got ready for bed.  Sam was really cold the night before, when I used my liner, so I loaned him my puffy.  I was mostly using it for my pillow anyway, and I figured I could work out some alternative method for that with some odds and ends.

As I lay in my sleeping bag, I hoped the weather would be clear and dry the next morning.  I really didn’t want to pack out in the rain. We would go over Kearsarge Pass and back down to Onion Valley to pick up Sam’s car.

Then what?  I committed to doing this blog, even if I didn’t succeed in completing the John Muir Trail.  And I had to admit, completing the trail was in doubt.  The cough and the mucus and the endless, endless, respiratory infection were getting more-and-more debilitating.

Mount Whitney and now Forester Pass are achievements, nothing to sneeze at. But I had hoped and dreamed of the John Muir trail for at least a year.  To abandon that now would really be disappointing.

We will just have to see what happens.  Tomorrow is another day.

#8353. It Took Six People and a Tractor to Haul This Massive Black Bear Off the Mountain

Published Oct 29, 2026 9:29 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Cecil Jackson, age 69, climbed into his elevated Millennium platform hunting blind the afternoon of October 24. It was opening day of archery bear season in this area of the Appalachian Mountains in southeast Kentucky. Jackson didn’t know it at the time, but he was about to take one of the biggest black bears in the area.

Archery deer season was also open and Jackson was going to take whatever the mountain provided.

“I was hunting deer or bear, whatever came along,” the just-retired Kentucky Utilities worker from the town of Pineville tells Outdoor Life. “I had trail cameras set up and I knew there were a few bears in the area. But I never imagined shooting a bear, because I had no gun with me in case I shot one and had to track it.”

Jackson’s blind was situated on rolling private farmland, and late that afternoon a fawn deer strolled down a mountain trail toward Jackson shortly before nightfall.

“It stood there awhile, then snapped its head up and looked up the mountain trail where it had come from,” Jackson says. “Then the deer left the area running. I thought maybe a buck was coming, but about 30 yards away a bear showed up.”

“That bear looked at me, turned to head after where the fawn had run, and that’s when I shot him with my Ravin crossbow,” Jackson says. “The bear ran about 100 yards, then turned into a thicket and I never saw or heard it again.”

The veteran hunter knew he’d made a good shot on the bear. He waited about 10 minutes in his blind, then went out and found his arrow, but there wasn’t much of a blood trail.

“Without a gun I wasn’t gonna track that bear alone,” he says. “That’s when a friend of mine called me and I told him I’d shot a bear, and I asked if he had a pistol with him.”

His buddy Tanner Jackson (no relation to Cecil) said he did have a gun and shortly met Cecil to start tracking the bear that night.

“I’m colorblind and have a tough time on a blood trail,” Cecil says. “We had a light, but it was a hard go trailing that bear.”

After about 70 yards of following faint blood sign, they stopped and used a high beam flashlight to scan the woods.

“I told Tanner to keep that pistol of his handy, and about that time I spotted the bear lying just off the woods path,” Cecil says. “I tossed a stick at it, but it didn’t move so we figured it was dead. When we walked up to it we couldn’t believe how big it was. We tried to lift just its head up but couldn’t.”

They phoned a nearby farm neighbor and some more friends. Using country woods savvy and a low spot in the road, they rigged a rope on a block and loaded the bear onto the tailgate of Jackson’s truck. They were just able to manhandle the whole bear into their truck.

“I didn’t think we could get that truck up and away from the low road spot, but that old truck in 4-wheel drive made it,” Cecil says. “It took six adults and a tractor to finally get that bear off the mountain.”

The hunters didn’t get the bear home until 11 p.m. that night.

The following day, James Dixon from the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources checked Cecil’s huge bear, which field dressed at an estimated weight of over 500 pounds. The bear measured 105-inches (nearly 9 feet) from nose to tail. Its neck measured 33 inches in circumference.

“James said he’d not seen a bear that size and believed it was the heaviest one taken so far from Kentucky this year – its huge head may be big enough for a record,” Cecil says. “I’m not much for bear meat, but some friends are, and I gave it all to them.

“I also gave away its fur to a buddy. But I may keep its skull for a European mount – especially if the head is of record size.”

#8347. Here’s What All Hunters Should Know About the Rut, Weather, and Deer Movement, According to One of the Top Experts In the Country

Published Oct 29, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

During the whitetail pre-rut and rut, hunters should worry less about the type of weather that will “get deer moving” and focus more on weather conditions that will help us hunt more effectively. That’s one of my takeaways from interviewing Dr. Grant Woods, a renowned wildlife researcher and diehard deer hunter. Woods and his crew publish excellent informational hunting content on his website, Growing Deer TV.

I interviewed him on Halloween just as a spectacular cold front was sinking into the heart of deer country. But if you didn’t kill your target buck during that front, don’t worry. The hunting is still getting better, Woods says. You can listen to my full interview with Woods in the podcast episode below. And read on to learn Woods’ other tips for understanding the rut, weather, and deer activity.

Recent research has found that fronts, even big cold fronts like we just experienced, don’t increase whitetail rutting activity, Woods says.

“The research says that weather is not much of a [factor in regards to deer rutting activity],” he says. “And that’s caused a bit of an issue in the last few years between hunters and researchers in a lot of online chatter.”

This discrepancy stems from the fact that hunters tend to see more deer when cold fronts hit. So, what gives? Woods’ explanation is essentially that both researchers and hunters are right. Cold temps don’t speed up breeding activity, but they do mean that hunters are more likely to see deer from their stands.

“I’m going to tell you, during our cold front, we went from high 70s to 30 and under in 24 hours. And on my trail cameras, when that cold front hit, I got a big spike… So what I’m saying is there’s some miscommunication going on,” Woods says. “Putting my scientist hat on now, typically I can’t publish something unless … 95 times out of 100 it’s going to happen. Well there’s a lot of conflicting things [concerning weather and deer activity]. When did the barometer rise? How much of a temperature was it? What phase of the rut was it? There’s a lot of noise. And when there’s a lot of noise a good biologist that’s doing really good work is going to say ‘I can’t say X because there’s too much noise.’ They’re going to be a little more conservative if they’re doing honest science.”

So what’s the takeaway for the hunter? It’s important to know that in the pre-rut deer usually don’t go running far outside their home range, even on a big cold front. However, they might walk around more within their home range.

Also, it’s important to understand what the pre-rut really is. Woods defines the pre-rut as the time period during which less than 25 percent of does are receptive. Bucks are seeking or moving more. Every day, a few more does become receptive and that brings a frenzy to the bucks. All of this happens regardless of weather.

Read Next: The Best Cellular Trail Cameras: The Complete Guide to Cell Cams and Subscription Plans

Yep, deer will keep on rutting even when the weather warms.

“The rut is a bell shaped curve and we’re definitively climbing up that curve [right now]. We’re increasing in intensity. So even if it’s 80 degrees, but the prom only happens once where you hunt, it’s still going to happen [during a warm front],” Woods says. “Now hunters sometimes debate that but if you look [at spring fawning season], fawns are born at the same time in the same place every year. There’s going to be some early fawns, a big cluster of fawns, and then some late fawns. [That’s because] especially up North, if they’re born too early, they’re going to fall into a snowbank and they’re not going to make it. And if they’re born too late they’re not going to gain enough weight before the next winter and they’re not going to make it. So the system is pretty refined over a long time. The rut is going to happen at the same time [locally, every year].”

Most deer hunters love to focus on the big fronts, but small changes in temperature can make for productive hunting, too. Woods uses a rough temperature change rule when deciding when to hunt vs. when to work.

“When it’s been warmer than normal, I get excited when there’s a 10 percent temperature decrease.”

So if it’s been 80 degrees and the forecast is calling for a drop down to 72 degrees, Woods will plan on hunting. During the late season, when deer are moving during warmer periods, Woods will hunt during a 10 percent increase in temperature. That means a small bump, like from 30 to 33 degrees.

When the rut is increasing in intensity, like it is right now, typical and stable weather makes for great hunting days, too, Woods says.

If the conditions are hot and not favorable, it’s probably not the time to skip work for an all-day sit. But Woods suggests making a short evening hunt and sliding in closer to bedding areas (assuming you can do so without bumping deer). This is because deer are likely to move only a few minutes before the end of legal shooting light during hot days. So there’s a chance you could catch a buck just leaving his bed at the end of the day.

Don’t be fooled by that one trail camera photo of a buck you have moving during a rainstorm. Bucks actually tend to move less during a steady rain.

“Researchers, again using GPS collared deer, have seen that bucks tend to move less when it’s raining,” Woods says. He thinks this could be because they have a harder time detecting predators in the rain, with blowing leaves and other disturbances in the woods.

Strangely, however, does tend to move a little bit more in the rain, Woods says. No one is quite sure why.

Instead of worrying about how weather impacts deer, hunters should consider how weather affects our potential success as predators. Woods mentions barometric pressure as a good example. During high pressure and low humidity, hunters tend to see more deer. But that’s not necessarily because deer are moving more on high-pressure days (data say they don’t). Instead, it’s likely because high pressure days favor the hunter so we’re not getting busted by deer.

“On high-pressure days, our scent is actually rising. So we’re able to get closer to deer without them detecting our scent,” Wood says. “We’re not talking [enough] about a hunter’s ability to hunt. We’re totally focused on the deer and what’s making them move. We need to accept that they’re feeding and drinking and avoiding predators every day of their lives.”

“I don’t have any data on this, but understanding the science and being a diehard hunter, I believe the biggest problem is that we often don’t include the human element and we are alerting way more deer than we think we are.”

Read Next: The 101 Best Tips for Hunting the Whitetail Rut

Wind is the biggest factor in our ability to hunt whitetails effectively—we all know this. But Woods says to analyze not just wind direction, but also wind speed and consistency. Hunters have the advantage during a strong (but not gusting) wind that is consistent in direction and speed.

This is one of the reasons why hunters tend to have success during cold fronts, Woods says. He suggests using NOAA’s Wind Roses page, which shows predominant wind direction and wind strength. This will help you get a better idea of how to set stands in your area.

Considering that deer live by their noses, Woods has a logical theory about why deer are most active at dawn and dusk. The temperature changes during morning (warming) and evening (cooling), often cause the wind to shift and swirl. A swirling wind helps deer detect predators from all directions, which makes them feel safer while moving and feeding.

“At night and full daytime deer only get nasal protection, if you will, from about 180 degrees —just throwing a number out,” Woods says. “But at sunrise and sunset, because the Earth is warming the Earth is cooling, thermals are shifting, they’re getting protection from a much greater area.”

One tactic Woods employs is executing very short hunts in the evening. The less time you’re out there, the less time there is for your scent to disperse and for that big buck to potentially bust you. —A.R.
